## What the provider cache actually does under fan-out

**The race is documented, not incidental.** Anthropic's prompt-caching page states it directly: "a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins. If you need cache hits for parallel requests, wait for the first response before sending subsequent requests." So when N agents fire simultaneously on a shared prefix, every one of them is a cache *miss* at admission time, and every one of them is billed `cache_creation` rather than `cache_read`. This is not a degradation to base input price — it is a *premium over* base input price, because the write multiplier is 1.25× (5-minute TTL) or 2.0× (1-hour TTL) while base is 1.0×.

We measured this in-house on 2026-08-14 (`scripts/xagent_billing_probe.py`, $1.08 live spend, `claude-haiku-4-5`): five callers on one fresh above-floor prefix, varying inter-arrival skew. At 0 ms skew, **5 of 5 callers billed `cache_creation`, zero reads**, replicated across both reps. At ≥1,000 ms skew, 1 writer and 4 readers, cleanly, both reps. The 50 ms and 200 ms cells disagreed between reps (5-vs-1 and 2-vs-5) — which is what a race should look like, but n=2 per cell bounds the transition without characterizing it. Caveats worth carrying: one model, and no invoice has been reconciled against these counters.

**Scoping.** Anthropic isolates caches **per workspace** on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, and Microsoft Foundry; Bedrock and Google Cloud isolate per **organization**. OpenAI states caches "are not shared between organizations," routed by `prompt_cache_key` with a hash of the prefix as secondary key. Two consequences for a gateway: pooling many customers into one workspace makes their prefixes mutually cache-visible (a privacy question, not just a cost one), and splitting customers into separate workspaces forfeits any cross-customer prefix sharing you might have been counting on.

**Cross-provider — this penalty is newly not Anthropic-specific.** OpenAI's current docs say GPT-5.6+ bills **cache writes at 1.25× and reads at 0.1×**, tracked as `cache_write_tokens`; earlier models had free writes at 0.1× reads. So the fan-out penalty has just arrived on OpenAI too. On free-write caches (older OpenAI models, Gemini implicit caching, which "automatically passes on cost savings" with no write charge), a concurrent fan-out costs you the *discount* but not a *premium* — a materially different failure mode.

## The arithmetic

Let `p` = base input $/token, `w` = write multiplier (1.25 or 2.0), `r` = 0.10 read multiplier, `P` = shared prefix tokens, `N` = parallel callers, `F` = the model's minimum cacheable prefix.

**Ideal (staggered) prefix cost ratio vs no caching** is `(w + r(N−1))/N`, so the saving fraction is `0.9 − 1.15/N` on the 5m tier. Break-even: `N > (w−r)/(1−r)` → **N ≥ 2 on the 5m tier, N ≥ 3 on the 1h tier**, and only if `P ≥ F`. Below the floor (512 tok on Opus 5 / Fable 5; 1,024 on Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6; 2,048 on Opus 4.7; 4,096 on Opus 4.6 and Haiku 4.5) the marker is a silent no-op — no error, no caching.

**Concurrent fan-out cost ratio is `w` — flat in both N and P.** It never breaks even. The prefix costs **+25% (5m) or +100% (1h)** more than sending nothing at all, at every N and every P. There is no N or P that rescues it; N and P only scale the size of the loss. This is the same mechanism as the depth-1 result we measured separately (+24.83% for a marked prefix with zero reads, flipping to −32.08% at k=2).

**The price of the race** — concurrent arm minus staggered arm — is `Δ = (N−1)·P·p·(w − r)`. On Claude Opus 5 ($5/MTok base) that is $5.75/MTok on the 5m tier and $9.50/MTok on the 1h tier:

| P (shared prefix) | N=4 | N=8 | N=16 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10k, 5m tier | $0.17 | $0.40 | $0.86 |
| 50k, 5m tier | $0.86 | $2.01 | $4.31 |
| 200k, 5m tier | $3.45 | $8.05 | $17.25 |
| 50k, **1h tier** | $1.42 | $3.33 | $7.13 |
| 200k, **1h tier** | $5.70 | $13.30 | $28.50 |

The 1h rows are the operative ones for a real coding agent: our 112-session field corpus shows **88.8% of writes bought the 1h tier**. A worked case — Opus 5, P=50k, per-caller suffix 2k, output 1.5k, N=8: no caching $2.380; staggered 5m cache $0.868 (−63.6%); concurrent 5m cache $2.880 (+21%); concurrent 1h cache $4.380 (+84%).

## Versus a cross-run store

Serving all N from one stored result costs `(P+S)p + O·q` — one execution — against the concurrent provider arm's `N·(P·p·w + S·p + O·q)`. With output at 5× input on every current Claude model (25/5, 10/2, 5/1) and P=50k, O=1.5k, that ratio is ≈**1.22N**: about 10× cheaper at N=8, and about 2.7× cheaper than even the perfectly staggered provider arm. The store wins at N=1 too (by ~22%), because it never marks anything and so never pays the 1.25× on a prefix that is not reused.

But state the limit plainly: **the store only serves all N from one result when the N reuse keys are equal.** Genuine fan-out — N callers with distinct suffixes over a shared prefix — produces N distinct keys and zero intra-fan-out hits. The store's N-fold win is on *duplicate* work (the same operation re-issued by different agents, or a repeat run), and on the *ancestor* operations that produced the shared prefix. On the fan-out layer itself, the provider prefix cache is the only mechanism that can touch P — and under concurrency it misfires.

The gap that leaves is small, real, and in the path: **single-flight the prefix.** Hold N−1 requests until the first response starts streaming (first token, not completion — TTL is measured from the *start* of the writing request, so a 4-minute first response eats nearly all of a 5-minute entry). Cost: one prefill of added latency. Value: `1.15·(N−1)·P·p` on the 5m tier, `1.90·(N−1)·P·p` on the 1h tier. Our 12-gateway audit found 0/12 doing anything in this class.

## Bottom line

- **Under simultaneous fan-out every caller pays the write.** Measured 5/5 writers at 0 ms skew, 1/5 at ≥1 s, replicated; Anthropic documents the cause ("a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins"). n=2/cell, one model — the 50–200 ms window is bounded, not characterized.
- **Concurrent fan-out never breaks even in N or P.** The prefix costs `w`× base — **+25% on the 5m tier, +100% on the 1h tier** — flat in N and flat in P. Only the *staggered* arm has a break-even, at **N ≥ 2 (5m) / N ≥ 3 (1h)**, and only for `P ≥ F` (512–4,096 tokens by model; below the floor the marker silently does nothing).
- **The 1h tier is the live case**: 88.8% of writes in our 112-session field corpus. At N=8, P=50k on Opus 5 the race costs $3.33 per fan-out; at N=16, P=200k, $28.50.
- **A store serving all N from one result is ~1.22N× cheaper** than the concurrent provider arm (≈10× at N=8) and ~2.7× cheaper than the staggered one — mostly because output tokens (5× input price) are cached by no provider. **But it only applies when the N reuse keys are identical**; distinct-suffix fan-out gets zero intra-fan-out hits from a Bazel-style store.
- **Scoping is workspace-level** (Claude API / Platform on AWS / Foundry) and **org-level** (Bedrock, Google Cloud, OpenAI) — pooling tenants shares caches; splitting them destroys sharing.
- **The penalty has just spread**: OpenAI GPT-5.6+ now bills writes at 1.25× / reads at 0.1×. On free-write caches (older OpenAI models, Gemini implicit) concurrency forfeits the discount but incurs no premium.
- **Estimated, not measured**: all dollar figures are rate-card arithmetic over vendor-reported counters; no invoice reconciled. The worked P/S/O values are illustrative, not sampled from customer traffic.

## What the providers actually shipped

**Anthropic.** Prompt caching entered public beta on the Claude API on **14 August 2024** ("Prompt caching is now available as a beta feature… reduce latency by up to 80% and costs by up to 90%" — [release notes](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/release-notes/api)), went GA around **17 December 2024**, and launched with a **5-minute** ephemeral TTL, a 1.25× cache-write multiplier and a 0.1× read multiplier. The **1-hour** tier ran as a beta (`extended-cache-ttl` header) and went **generally available on 13 August 2025**: "The 1-hour cache duration for prompt caching is now generally available. You can now use the extended cache TTL without a beta header." Prices have not moved since: today's [pricing page](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing) lists 5m writes at **1.25×**, 1h writes at **2×**, hits and refreshes at **0.1×** base input — e.g. Claude Opus 5 at $5 / $6.25 / $10 / $0.50 per MTok. The [caching docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) still say "Currently, `ephemeral` is the only supported cache type." **Anthropic has no tier longer than one hour and has publicly signalled none.** Scope has narrowed in specificity rather than broadened: "Caches are isolated per workspace within an organization on the Claude API… Bedrock and Google Cloud use organization-level isolation only," and "Different organizations never share caches, even if they use identical prompts." What Anthropic *has* shipped instead is friction removal — automatic caching (19 Feb 2026), cache diagnostics beta (13 May 2026), mid-conversation system messages and mid-conversation tool changes that preserve the cache across turns, and a 1,024-token minimum on Opus 4.8. That is the same competitive surface a third-party reuse layer sells into, being closed for free.

**OpenAI.** Automatic prompt caching launched **1 October 2024** ("Discounts and faster processing times on recently seen input tokens" — [changelog](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/changelog)); the launch discount was 50% off cached input, which I am stating from memory and could not re-verify (the help-center article 403s and my search budget was exhausted). Today the [caching guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) states "**Cached input tokens are billed at 0.1× the uncached input token rate**" — so the read discount roughly doubled over two years. The TTL history is the important part:

- Default in-memory behaviour: "cached prefixes generally remain active for **5 to 10 minutes of inactivity, up to a maximum of one hour**."
- **13 November 2025**: OpenAI "Released extended prompt cache retention. Extended prompt cache retention keeps cached prefixes active for longer, **up to a maximum of 24 hours**" — set via `prompt_cache_retention: "24h"`, supported on gpt-4.1, gpt-5, gpt-5-codex, the gpt-5.1 family, gpt-5.2, gpt-5.4, gpt-5.5 and gpt-5.5-pro.
- Price for the 24h tier: **zero premium**. "For models that support both in-memory and extended retention, prompt cache pricing is the same for both policies." No storage fee.
- **24 April 2026**: "Caching for GPT-5.5 only works with extended prompt caching. In-memory prompt caching is not supported" — i.e. 24h became the *only* mode on that model.
- **29 May 2026**: "For organizations without ZDR enabled, `prompt_cache_retention` now defaults to `24h` instead of `in_memory`, enabling extended prompt caching by default."

So the hypothetical in the brief — "what would happen if a provider shipped a 24 hour cache tier" — is not hypothetical. It shipped nine months ago, at no extra cost, and became the silent default eleven weeks ago.

The counter-current matters too, and it is genuinely surprising: the **GPT-5.6 family (released 9 July 2026)** dropped extended retention entirely. GPT-5.6 uses `prompt_cache_options.ttl` where "the only supported value is `30m`, which is also the default," and GPT-5.6 appears nowhere in the extended-retention model list. The 30-minute lifetime "begins when the prefix is written and refreshes whenever the prefix is reused." OpenAI's newest and most expensive family therefore has a *shorter* maximum cache life than the one it replaced. TTL is a knob tied to KV-cache storage economics per model architecture, and it moves in both directions.

**Google.** Explicit context caching launched with Gemini 1.5 in **May 2024**. Implicit caching arrived **8 May 2025** for Gemini 2.5, "the same 75% token discount," with minimums cut to 1,024 tokens (2.5 Flash) and 2,048 (2.5 Pro) ([blog](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/gemini-2-5-models-now-support-implicit-caching/)). That 75% has since become **90%**: current [pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing) shows Gemini 3.7 Flash input $0.75 vs cached $0.075, 3.5 Flash $1.50 vs $0.15, 2.5 Pro $1.25 vs $0.125 — all three providers have now converged on a 0.1× read multiplier. Google is the outlier on TTL: explicit caching's `ttl` "defaults to 1 hour" if unset and **no maximum is documented** ([caching docs](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/generate-content/caching)). You can already buy a 7-day cache from Google today. It is priced as rent: **$0.50/MTok/hour** (3.7/3.6 Flash), **$1.00** (3.5 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, 2.5 Flash), **$4.50** (2.5 Pro).

That rent is why unbounded TTL has not eaten anyone's lunch. Holding 1 MTok across a 24-hour idle gap on Gemini 3.5 Flash costs **$24.00** in storage to save **$1.35** on the read that follows — about 18× underwater. On 2.5 Pro it is $108 to save $1.13, roughly 96× underwater. Google's long-TTL cache is economically a short-horizon tool wearing a long-horizon interface. OpenAI's 24h tier is the genuinely dangerous one precisely because it charges no rent at all.

## How exposed is a business built on the 1h→cross-day gap?

Severely, if that gap is the actual product. The gap now exists on exactly one of three providers. On OpenAI it is closed, free, and default-on for every non-ZDR org — a customer gets cross-day prefix reuse by doing nothing, and a vendor selling it there is selling something already in the box. On Google it is closed on paper and open in practice, but the practical opening is a rent-arbitrage window, not a technology gap, and it will close the moment Google decides KV storage is cheap enough to give away as OpenAI did. Only Anthropic still sits at a hard 1-hour ceiling, and Anthropic is the provider whose customers are most concentrated in exactly the long-running coding-agent workload where cross-day reuse would pay. A single Anthropic release-note line — "24-hour cache duration is now available" — would remove the last provider where the pitch lands. Nothing in the release notes signals it; that is weak evidence of safety, since OpenAI's own 24h tier appeared with no advance signal at all.

Two things blunt the exposure, and they are worth separating from wishful thinking. First, our own field measurement (internal, not citable) found 97.47% cache hit rates on real receipts with **99.86% of cache value coming from within-session continuation**, and the TTL cliff sitting at 1h rather than 5m. If that holds, the cross-day prefix gap was never where the money was — which means low exposure, but only because there was little revenue there to lose. Second, and more durably: every provider mechanism discussed here discounts **input tokens only**. A cache hit costs 0.1× input; output tokens are billed in full every time, and the model still runs. The operation-level reuse store described in the brief is a different object — it returns the *output* of a completed operation without a model call, covers non-model operations (test runs, file reads, HTTP fetches) that no provider ever sees, keys on a DAG rather than a contiguous prefix so it survives reordering, and invalidates on artifact change rather than on a wall clock. No provider TTL change touches any of that. A vendor whose receipts are denominated in avoided output tokens and avoided tool executions is not in the TTL business; a vendor whose receipts are denominated in converted input tokens is, and the ceiling on that business is the residual 0.1× the provider already gave away.

**Bottom line**

- **The 24h scenario already happened.** OpenAI shipped `prompt_cache_retention: "24h"` on **13 Nov 2025** at **no price premium**, made it mandatory on GPT-5.5 (**24 Apr 2026**), and made it the **default** for non-ZDR orgs (**29 May 2026**).
- **Google already sells unbounded TTL** (explicit cache, default 1h, no documented max) but charges **$0.50–$4.50 per MTok per hour** of storage — bridging a 24h gap runs ~18× (3.5 Flash) to ~96× (2.5 Pro) underwater versus the read it saves.
- **Anthropic is the last 1-hour holdout**: 5m write 1.25×, 1h write 2×, read 0.1×, "`ephemeral` is the only supported cache type," no longer tier signalled — and it is the provider where the cross-day pitch most needs to land.
- **The trend is not monotonic.** GPT-5.6 (**9 Jul 2026**) reverted to a **30-minute-only** exact TTL and dropped 24h support entirely. TTL tracks per-architecture KV storage cost, so it can shorten as easily as lengthen.
- **Read prices converged on 0.1×** everywhere (Anthropic since Aug 2024; OpenAI up from ~50%; Google from 75% in May 2025 to 90% today). The input-side residual a reuse layer can still capture is capped at ~10% of input price.
- **Anthropic is closing the adjacent surface for free** — automatic caching (19 Feb 2026), cache diagnostics (13 May 2026), cache-preserving mid-conversation tool and system-message changes. Cache *tuning* as a product is being commoditized independently of TTL.
- **Defensible position:** price the product on avoided output tokens and avoided tool executions with correctness-keyed invalidation, not on converted input tokens. Prefix TTL changes cannot reach the former. Any pitch deck slide whose headline is "providers only cache for an hour" should be treated as a dated liability, not an asset.

## Shadow-cost of a reuse layer

### What a shadow check actually buys

A shadow recomputation that runs *after* (or concurrently with) serving the stored result does not prevent the stale answer from being used — it only measures how often that happens. So the shadow layer buys **evidence, not correctness**. If you want prevention you have to recompute before serving, which is just not reusing. This matters for how you price it: the shadow rate is the cost of a *bound you can quote*, and it should be justified against whatever the bound is worth (an audit claim, a billing guarantee), not against avoided errors. Detection lag is the other half of that: at shadow rate *r* and true staleness *s*, the expected number of hits served before the first mismatch is caught is 1/(rs) — 333 hits at r=30%, s=1%; 10,000 hits at r=1%, s=1%.

### Sizing the check: it's a fixed count per window, not a rate

The right statistical object is a one-sided binomial upper bound. Draw *n* hits uniformly at random from the hit stream, recompute, compare. With **zero** mismatches observed, the Clopper–Pearson upper bound gives n = ln(1−c)/ln(1−s), which for small *s* is the familiar rule of three, ≈ 3/s at 95% ([Clopper & Pearson 1934](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/26.4.404); [Hanley & Lippman-Hand 1983](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1983.03330370053031)):

| confidence | s ≤ 5% | s ≤ 1% | s ≤ 0.5% | s ≤ 0.1% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 90% | 45 | 230 | 460 | 2,302 |
| 95% | 59 | 299 | 598 | 2,995 |
| 99% | 90 | 459 | 919 | 4,603 |

Two corrections make this much more expensive in practice. First, **you will observe mismatches**, and the zero-failure numbers collapse the moment you do. To hold a 95% upper bound of 1% when the true rate is 0.5%, you need n ≈ 1,095 (3.7× the zero-failure count); at a true rate of 0.75% you need n ≈ 4,325 (14.5×). The count blows up hyperbolically as the true rate approaches the bound, which is the honest way of saying *you cannot certify a bound you are actually near*. Second, **reuse keys are not exchangeable**. A pooled sample bounds the aggregate rate only; if you want the bound per operation class (file read vs HTTP fetch vs DB query vs test run), you pay ~299 per class. Six classes is ~1,794 checks per window.

The consequential move is that this is a **count per validity window**, not a rate — and the world changes, so the bound must be re-earned every window. The rate is n·k/H where H is hits served per window:

| strata | H=300 | H=1,000 | H=10,000 | H=100,000 | H=1,000,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| k=1 (n=299) | 99.7% | 29.9% | 2.99% | 0.30% | 0.03% |
| k=6 (n=1,794) | 100% | 100% | 17.9% | 1.79% | 0.18% |

So the audit is a fixed tax that amortizes with volume. A deployment serving a few hundred reuse hits a day cannot buy a 1%/95% bound at any price short of recomputing everything — the layer is statistically worthless at small scale, and *worthless* here is not rhetoric, it's r ≥ 1.

One large saving is available and it's structural rather than statistical: because the key composes transitively, a pure operation cannot go stale — its output is determined by inputs whose hashes are already in the key. Staleness enters only at **leaves that read the outside world** and at **hidden inputs you failed to hash** (env vars, tool versions, locale, machine). The shadow check is therefore a *hermeticity audit*, and its population is the leaf set, not all operations. This is exactly the failure mode Bazel answers with sandboxing and Nix with content-addressed inputs; the shadow rate is the price of not having done that.

### Nondeterministic operations break the whole design

Model calls at temperature > 0 disagree with themselves. A shadow comparison then measures *staleness + resampling noise*, so you need a two-proportion test against a fresh-vs-fresh baseline arm, at n ≈ (z_α+z_β)²[p₀(1−p₀)+p₁(1−p₁)]/s² per arm:

| fresh-vs-fresh disagreement p₀ | detect s=5% | detect s=1% |
|---|---|---|
| 2% | 216 | 3,124 |
| 10% | 654 | 14,284 |
| 20% | 1,324 | 31,374 |
| 40% | 3,333 | 82,643 |

At two arms — and the baseline arm costs two executions, so ~3n recomputes — bounding staleness at 1% on an operation with 20% intrinsic disagreement costs on the order of **90,000 recomputations per window**. That is not a shadow rate, it is a full re-run of the workload several times over. The practical consequence: the sharpness of your equivalence predicate, not your sampling budget, sets the tightest bound you can afford. If you can define a predicate under which fresh-vs-fresh passes ~always, you are back in the deterministic table; if you can't, don't claim a staleness bound on model calls at all.

### Converting the rate into a cost — the naive answer, and why it's wrong

Normalize the cost of executing an operation to 1. With hit rate *h*, shadow rate *r*, and *w* the store's own overhead (lookup, write, serialization, storage) as a fraction of an execution:

**S = h(1−r)(1−ε) − w**, break-even at **r\* = 1 − w / [h(1−ε)]**

| h | w=1% | w=5% | w=15% |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | 98.9% | 94.4% | 83.2% |
| 0.7 | 98.6% | 92.8% | 78.4% |
| 0.5 | 98.0% | 89.9% | 69.7% |
| 0.3 | 96.6% | 83.2% | 49.5% |
| 0.1 | 89.9% | 49.5% | −51.5% |

Read naively this says shadow cost is a non-issue: at h=0.7 you can shadow 93% of hits and still break even. That answer is wrong, because it prices against an uncached baseline. The task states the correct baseline: **provider prefix caching already on and tuned** — automatic and free at [Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) (reads at 0.1×, writes 1.25×/5m and 2×/1h), [OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) (0.1× cached input, automatic ≥1,024 tokens), and [Google](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching) (implicit caching on by default for Gemini 2.5+).

That baseline creates a second-order term the naive model misses entirely: **serving from the reuse store suppresses the provider cache.** Every hit is a request that doesn't go to the provider, so inter-request gaps stretch and the provider's prefix entry ages toward its TTL. Our own field measurement over 112 real sessions and 9,224 billed requests (`/Users/jamesyang/Documents/GitHub/Brevitas-Systems/docs/FIELD_CACHE_MEASUREMENT.md`) prices this: the cliff sits at 3600s with a 72.7% loss rate past it, and caching was worth 84.1% of the bill ($1,212 billed vs $7,601 counterfactual). Define γ = cold-execution cost / warm-execution cost. Measured all-in, γ = 6.27; on the input line alone at the rate card it is 12.5 (5m tier) to 20 (1h tier).

Let q = the share of reuse hits that push a downstream execution over the TTL it would otherwise have made. Then S = h(1−r)[1 − q(γ−1)] − w, and the layer is net-negative regardless of shadow rate once **q > 1/(γ−1)**: 19.0% at γ=6.27, 8.7% at γ=12.5, 5.3% at γ=20. Roughly one induced cold miss cancels five to nineteen reuse hits.

The twist is that a **shadow recomputation is a real execution, so it refreshes the provider prefix.** Modelling q(r) = q₀(1−r) and writing u = 1−r gives S(u) = h·u − h·q₀(γ−1)u² − w — a downward parabola with an interior optimum at u\* = 1/[2q₀(γ−1)] whenever q₀(γ−1) > ½. The shadow check partly pays for itself. With γ=6.27, w=3%, h=0.7:

| q₀ | cost-optimal r | max saving | viable r window |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.02 | 0% | 0.60 | 0 – 95.7% |
| 0.05 | 0% | 0.49 | 0 – 95.7% |
| 0.10 | 5.1% | 0.30 | 0 – 95.6% |
| 0.20 | 52.6% | 0.14 | **9.6% – 95.5%** |
| 0.40 | 76.3% | 0.05 | **57.3% – 95.2%** |

So break-even is not a single threshold but a **window**: too little shadowing and TTL suppression eats the saving; too much and recomputation does. The q₀ column is an estimate, not a measurement — the field arrival distribution (93.7% of gaps ≤ 300s, 1.1% > 1h) makes small q₀ plausible at moderate h and rising steeply as h → 1, but nobody has measured it directly and it is the single parameter this whole conclusion turns on.

---

**Bottom line**

- **Shadow checking buys a bound, not correctness** — a post-hoc recompute cannot stop the stale answer it detects; expect 1/(rs) hits served before the first catch (10,000 at r=1%, s=1%).
- **The requirement is ~300 recomputes per stratum per validity window** (95%/1%, zero mismatches), so the *rate* is 30% at 1,000 hits/window and 0.3% at 100,000 — small deployments cannot buy a tight bound at any affordable rate. Observing real mismatches multiplies the count 4–15×.
- **Shadow only the leaves.** Pure operations can't go stale under a transitive key; staleness lives at world-reading leaves and un-hashed hidden inputs. The shadow rate is the price of imperfect hermeticity (Bazel/Nix's sandboxing and content-addressing are the alternative).
- **Nondeterministic model calls are effectively unbindable** — separating s=1% from 20% intrinsic disagreement needs ~31k samples per arm (~90k recomputes). The equivalence predicate, not the budget, sets the achievable bound.
- **Naive break-even is r\* = 1 − w/[h(1−ε)]**, i.e. 78–99% for realistic h and overhead — which is why the naive model is misleading.
- **Against a provider-prefix-cached baseline the binding constraint is TTL suppression, not the shadow rate.** With γ (cold/warm) = 6.27 measured (12.5–20 on the input line), the layer is negative once >19% (or >5–9%) of hits push a downstream call past the TTL — a limit reached independently of any shadow spend.
- **Because shadow recomputes keep the provider cache warm, the cost-optimal shadow rate can be strictly positive** — 53% at q₀=0.2, with a viable window of ~10–95%. The statistically-required rate and the cost-optimal rate can coincide, which is the one genuinely favourable result here.
- **Caveats:** γ is measured single-subject (112 Claude Code sessions, one user, rate-card arithmetic, no invoice reconciled); q₀ is estimated, not measured, and is the parameter the conclusion is most sensitive to; the quadratic q(r) = q₀(1−r) is a modelling choice.

## Capture rate: what share of a model-spend saving is actually billable

### The three pricing archetypes, and what they really cost

### Converting all of this to a common unit

The per-request meters look tiny until you convert them to a share of the bill they sit beside. Assume an average billable request of roughly $0.05 (a mid-size Claude request — say 20k input and 2k output on Opus at $5/$25 per MTok is about $0.15, and a cache-heavy continuation is far less; **this is my estimate, not a published figure**, and it swings the result linearly). Then a customer at $100k/mo of model spend is issuing about 2M requests, and:

- Portkey at $0.00009/request → ~$180/mo → **0.18% of spend**
- TrueFoundry at $0.00025–0.0005 → $500–1,000/mo → **0.5–1.0% of spend**
- Datadog LLM Observability at $0.00035/span → $700/mo → **0.7% of spend** (more if you emit several spans per request)
- Langfuse at $0.00007/unit → $140/mo → **0.14% of spend**

That is the same band Datadog charges for cloud cost management (0.50–1.00% of spend under management) and the same band Vantage's flat tiers land in at their ceilings. The convergence is the single most useful finding here: **LLM infrastructure that sits beside the spend, rather than intermediating it, prices at roughly 0.2–1.0% of that spend.** The only vendors above that band are the ones that take custody of the money — Requesty at 5%, Cloudflare at 5% on credits, OpenRouter at 5% on BYOK above a generous free allowance — and even they explicitly disclaim markup on inference itself.

Now express the same thing as a share of savings, which is the question actually asked. The bridge is arithmetic: *capture rate as % of savings = (fee as % of spend) ÷ (savings as % of spend)*. A tool that cuts 20% off the bill and charges 25% of savings is taking 5% of spend. The same tool charging 1% of spend is taking 5% of savings. That is a tenfold difference in revenue for identical delivered value, decided entirely by the meter.

### Why contingent pricing is not available to a cross-run reuse layer

Contingent pricing captures 5–10x more per dollar of savings than the flat models. But every vendor that actually gets it shares one property: **the saving is settled by the provider's own invoice.** ProsperOps says so in the sentence quoted above — *"as determined by your provider's billing system."* Archera's 2–30% is levied on commitment discounts that appear as line items on the AWS bill. Neither vendor is asserting a counterfactual; both are pointing at a number the customer's provider computed.

A cross-run reuse layer cannot do this. The saving is definitionally counterfactual — the tokens you did not send. Anthropic's invoice shows what you spent; there is no line on it for the operation that was served from the store instead of executed. That removes the settlement mechanism that makes 25–30% defensible, and it means any contingent invoice is the vendor grading its own homework. (This repo's own roadmap reaches the same conclusion from the audit-independence angle: SEC Rule 2-01(b) disqualifies anyone reviewing their own work, and the ESCO answer is to freeze the measurement protocol ex ante under a third party rather than to claim auditor status.)

Two further deflationary facts bear directly on the size of the saving being split. First, the baseline the question stipulates is not hypothetical: Anthropic's prompt caching charges cache reads at ~0.1x base input and cache writes at 1.25x (5-minute TTL) or 2x (1-hour TTL), breaking even at two requests on the short TTL and three on the long one — and it is free. Second, breakpoint placement, the thing a reuse layer would most obviously sell, has been commoditized: Anthropic ships top-level `cache_control` that auto-advances the breakpoint, Vercel's gateway does automatic caching at zero markup, and Cloudflare's gateway includes caching in its free tier. The measured field data in this repo puts the field cache hit rate at 97.47% with 99.86% of cache value sitting in within-session continuation — which the provider's own TTL already covers. So the incremental saving a cross-run store adds over a tuned provider cache is small, and its floor is set by competitors charging zero for the adjacent capability.

### What a reuse layer could realistically charge

The defensible position is the non-contingent one, metered on spend under management, tiered, with a savings-linked ceiling that neutralizes the obvious objection ("you're paid while I waste money"). That is precisely what the tier table already in `docs/ROADMAP_2026-08-14.md` proposes, and it lands on top of the only public anchor in the market:

|---|---|---|---|
| Free | ≤$5k/mo | 0% | — |
| Team | $5k–100k | 1.5% | $299/mo |
| Business | $100k–500k | 1.0% | $1,500/mo |

with a hard cap that the fee never exceeds 25% of verified savings in the same period.

**Revenue per customer** (my computation from those tiers; the *rates* are a proposal, not a published price):

- **$10,000/mo spend.** Marginal fee is $5,000 × 1.5% = $75, so the $299 floor binds. **$299/mo, $3,588/yr — an effective 2.99% of spend.** The floor, not the rate, is doing all the work at this size, exactly as Vantage's 2.7%-at-the-floor behaviour predicts. For the 25%-of-savings cap not to bite, the layer must be provably saving ≥$1,196/mo, i.e. **~12% of the bill** — a very demanding bar for incremental savings over an already-tuned prefix cache.
- **$100,000/mo spend.** $95,000 × 1.5% = **$1,425/mo, $17,100/yr — 1.43% of spend.** The cap requires ≥$5,700/mo of verified savings, ~5.7% of the bill.
- **$1,000,000/mo spend.** $95k×1.5% + $400k×1.0% + $500k×0.5% = **$7,925/mo, $95,100/yr — 0.79% of spend.** The cap requires ≥$31,700/mo of savings, ~3.2% of the bill — the easiest bar of the three.

For comparison, the same three customers under the alternatives. At a contingent 25% of savings, with incremental savings at 3% of the bill (**my estimate**, and this repo's own measurements suggest cross-run warming can be net-negative against the 1-hour tier, so 3% is not conservative): $75, $750, $7,500/mo. At 10% incremental savings: $250, $2,500, $25,000/mo. At pure per-request pricing in the observed 0.2–1.0% band: $20–100, $200–1,000, $2,000–10,000/mo. All three models converge near ~$8–10k/mo at the $1M customer and diverge wildly at the $10k customer, where floors dominate everything.

Two consequences follow. The percentage is not the lever — the floor is; a 200-customer book on these tiers is ~$2.1M ARR, of which ten large accounts are a third of revenue and the long tail of Team accounts is a quarter of revenue for most of the support load. And the cap binds inversely to customer size, which means the "25% of savings" ceiling is a marketing asset at the enterprise end and a genuine constraint at the small end.

## Cross-provider prompt caching, and what it leaves on the table

**Short answer: yes, the answer depends heavily on the provider — but not on the axis people expect.** Automatic-vs-opt-in has almost stopped mattering (caching is now on by default nearly everywhere). What actually varies, by more than an order of magnitude, is (1) how long a cache survives relative to the gap between runs, and (2) how much of the residual bill is left after the discount. Those two numbers set the reuse layer's headroom, and they are not correlated.

### Where the reuse layer has the most headroom

**Anthropic and OpenAI on frontier models.** Both have short TTLs relative to any realistic cross-run gap. Our own field data on 112 real Claude Code sessions (9,224 billed requests, 2.49B prompt tokens) shows P(inter-request gap > 1 h) = 1.1% *within* a session — meaning provider caching is already capturing essentially all intra-session value (97.47% of prompt tokens billed at the 0.10× rate, 84.1% saved vs. no cache). But a run repeated tomorrow is 100% outside every Anthropic and OpenAI TTL, and the repeat run then pays **1.25× or 2×**, not 1.0×, to re-warm. The reuse layer's competition there is literally nothing.

Two sharpeners, both from our live probes: (a) at genuinely simultaneous fan-out (0 ms skew, 5 callers on one fresh prefix) **all five callers were billed a cache write** — the provider cache degenerates to 5 × 1.25× with zero reads, whereas one stored result serves all five; (b) marking a prefix that is reused only once costs **+24.8%**, so the provider mechanism is actively negative in exactly the one-shot regime a reuse store handles best.

**Gemini explicit caching is the single largest priced gap.** Google is the only vendor that will hold a prefix for a day — and charges $4.50 per 1M tokens per hour to do it on 3.1 Pro. Holding 1M tokens for 24 h costs **$108**, against $0.20 to simply re-read them once cached. Cross-run persistence at the provider is priced roughly **500× above** the re-read it replaces. Any local store beats that trivially. (Estimate flag: that ratio is my arithmetic on their two published rates, not a Google figure.)

**Fireworks serverless, on a per-token basis.** A 50% discount leaves twice the residual that a 0.10× discount leaves, so per cached token there is more to capture — though absolute prices are low enough that it rarely dominates.

### Where it has the least

**DeepSeek.** Automatic, zero write premium, ~97% read discount, and a documented lifetime of *hours to days* — that is already a cross-run reuse layer, given away free, with no integration. Residual is output tokens only, and at $0.66–$1.98 per 1M output the absolute dollars are ~10–25× below Opus-class. Worth flagging as a change since our 2026‑08‑10 probe: **peak/off-peak pricing is now live** (2× during 01:00–04:00 and 06:00–10:00 UTC), so time-shifting has become a real lever there and cache-reuse a smaller one.

**Self-hosted vLLM/SGLang.** Prefix caching is on by default, has no TTL at all (LRU only), and HiCache/LMCache already offer cross-run persistence to CPU/disk. Critically there is **no per-token bill**, so a savings-share product has nothing to compute a counterfactual against. The value is GPU-seconds and latency, owned by the customer.

### Could one product serve both?

**Yes — but only if the product is operation-level memoization plus a receipt, not prefix shaping.** The reuse-key mechanism (type + literal args + model id + sampling params + artifact content hashes + upstream output hashes) is entirely provider-agnostic; nothing in it touches cache semantics. What varies is the *counterfactual you can bill*: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek and Fireworks all report cached vs. uncached token counts in the usage receipt, so a dollar figure is derivable; vLLM/SGLang emit none. That splits commercially, not technically — savings-share on metered APIs, flat license on self-hosted where the pitch is latency and capacity.

The part that genuinely does *not* port is the shaping layer, and our own measurements say to drop it anyway: shaping over a competent native-caching customer measured **−30.8% on Anthropic and −1.3% on DeepSeek**. Removing it makes the product more portable, not less. The remaining per-provider work is a thin adapter: floors (512–4,096 tokens on Anthropic by model, 1,024–2,048 on OpenAI, 2,048–4,096 on Gemini, ~128-token blocks measured on DeepSeek) and receipt field names.

One correctness constraint is also cross-provider: every vendor states outputs stay randomized under prefix caching, so memoizing a *model* call changes semantics in a way memoizing a *tool* call does not. The reuse layer needs a per-operation-type policy — and conveniently, tool calls are both the safest to memoize and the one class no provider caches at all.

- **Automatic-vs-opt-in is no longer a differentiator** — default-on at OpenAI, Gemini (implicit), DeepSeek, Fireworks, vLLM and SGLang; only Anthropic still requires a field on the request.
- **TTL is the differentiator.** Minutes-to-1h at Anthropic/OpenAI/Gemini-implicit/Fireworks vs. **hours-to-days at DeepSeek** vs. **unbounded-but-LRU** self-hosted. Cross-run reuse lives entirely in that gap.
- **Read discounts have converged on 0.10×** (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini) with two outliers: DeepSeek ~**0.03×** and Fireworks serverless **0.50×**.
- **Write premiums exist only at Anthropic (1.25×/2×) and OpenAI GPT‑5.6+ (1.25×)** — and they mean a cold repeat run pays *more* than list, which is upside for a reuse store.
- **Nobody does result-level caching, and nobody caches tool calls.** That is the reuse layer's uncontested surface on every provider.
- **Most headroom:** Anthropic/OpenAI frontier models (short TTL, write premium, concurrent fan-out makes all N callers pay the write) and **Gemini explicit caching**, where provider-side persistence is priced ~500× above a re-read.
- **Least headroom:** **DeepSeek** (already a free multi-day cross-run cache at ~97% off) and **self-hosted vLLM/SGLang** (default-on, no TTL, no bill line to discount).
- **One product works** if it ships as provider-agnostic operation memoization + receipt-derived proof, with a thin per-provider adapter for floors and receipt fields — two pricing models (savings-share vs. flat), not two products.

## Costing a persistent cross-run reuse store

### Method and assumptions

I priced against the **AWS Price List API** rather than the HTML pricing pages, because those pages render their tables in JavaScript and return nothing extractable. The API is the same source of truth that feeds them, and each file carries a publication date — S3 `2026-08-07`, DynamoDB `2026-08-15`, ElastiCache `2026-08-13`, RDS `2026-08-12`, Data Transfer `2026-07-20`. GCS, R2 and Upstash came from their published pages. Everything is us-east-1 / us-central1, on-demand, no committed-use discounts.

Four things are **my assumptions, not measured facts**, and every number below moves with them: an average operation output of **4 KB**; a **70% hit rate** on a repeat run (so 30% of operations write a new entry); a **30-day retention window**, which puts the steady-state resident set at one month of writes; and a **read on every operation** whether it hits or misses — you must look up the key before you know. The last one matters more than it sounds, and I'll come back to it.

### The structural result: this is a request-priced workload, not a storage-priced one

At 100M operations/month on S3 Standard, the bill decomposes like this:

| Component | Cost/mo | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Storage (114 GB resident) | $2.63 | 1.2% |
| PUTs (30M writes @ $0.005/1,000) | $150.00 | 69.2% |
| GETs (100M lookups @ $0.0004/1,000) | $40.00 | 18.5% |
| Egress to internet (267 GB @ $0.09/GB) | $24.03 | 11.1% |
| **Total** | **$216.66** | |

Storage is 1.2% of a storage bill. The name of the cost line is wrong. Three consequences follow directly:

**Retention length is nearly free.** Going from 30 days to 12 months multiplies the resident set 12× — 114 GB to 1,373 GB — and raises the total bill from $217 to $246, a 13% increase. If cross-week reuse is the point, buy cross-*year* reuse; it costs almost nothing. The expensive thing is the per-operation lookup, and that doesn't change with retention.

**Every cold-storage instinct is actively wrong here.** S3 Standard-IA, One Zone-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval all bill a **minimum of 128 KB per object** ([AWS storage classes doc](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html), which states it explicitly in the comparison table). On a 4 KB object that's a 32× inflation: Standard-IA's list $0.0125/GB-mo becomes an effective **$0.40/GB-mo**, 17× *more expensive* than S3 Standard's $0.023. Glacier IR's $0.004 becomes $0.128. Intelligent-Tiering doesn't help either — objects under 128 KB aren't monitored and stay in the Frequent Access tier permanently, so you pay the monitoring fee for nothing. GCS has no equivalent minimum-object-size rule (only minimum *duration*: 30/90/365 days), so it degrades more gracefully, but Nearline's saving is on a line item that's 1% of the bill.

**Optimize requests, and the picture changes a lot.** Comparing backends at 100M ops/month:

| Backend | Storage | Writes | Reads | Egress | **Total** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| S3 Express One Zone | $12.59 | $34.27 | $3.16 | $24.03 | **$74** |
| Cloudflare R2 | $1.72 | $135.00 | $36.00 | $0 | **$173** |
| DynamoDB on-demand | $28.61 | $93.75 | $12.50 | $24.03 | **$159** |
| GCS Standard | $2.29 | $150.00 | $40.00 | ~$24 | **~$216** |
| S3 Standard | $2.63 | $150.00 | $40.00 | $24.03 | **$217** |

S3 Express One Zone wins by ~3× despite storage costing 4.8× more per GB, because its request prices are the outlier: $0.00113 per 1,000 PUTs and $0.00003 per 1,000 GETs, versus $0.005 and $0.0004 on Standard. It's single-AZ, which for a *recomputable* cache is exactly the right durability trade — losing an AZ costs you a cache miss, not data. R2's zero egress is worth $24/mo here; it matters far more if your agents run outside the cloud holding the store. DynamoDB reads are startlingly cheap ($0.125 per million RRU, halved for eventually-consistent reads, which is fine for immutable content-addressed data) but writes bill per KB, so a 4 KB item costs 5 write units.

### Scaling down: the floor eats the small tier

| Ops/month | Resident | S3 Standard | Express One Zone | R2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 12 MB | $0.02 | $0.01 | $0.02 |
| 1,000,000 | 1.1 GB | $2.17 | $0.74 | $1.73 |
| 100,000,000 | 114 GB | $216.66 | $74.05 | $173.00 |

At 10k operations/month the marginal cost is two cents, which is not a real number — you can't operate a service on two cents. The honest cost at that tier is whatever fixed infrastructure you attach. And this is where the design decision bites: **if you use the content hash as the object key, you need no separate index at all** — a miss is a 404 GET, billed as an ordinary request, and the index cost is $0. If instead you stand up a managed index or hot tier, the floors are brutal at low volume:

- RDS PostgreSQL `db.t4g.medium`, single-AZ: **$47.45/mo** ($0.065/hr)
- RDS `db.m7g.large`, single-AZ: **$122.64/mo** ($0.168/hr), plus $0.115/GB-mo for gp3
- ElastiCache `cache.r7g.large`: **$127.90/mo** ($0.1752/hr) for 13.07 GiB = $9.79/GB-mo
- ElastiCache Serverless Valkey: **$0.084 per GB-hour = $61.32 per GB-month**, plus $0.0023 per million ECPUs
- Upstash Redis pay-as-you-go: $2.00 per million commands, $0.25/GB-mo (no floor — the only genuinely usage-priced Redis here)

Serverless Valkey at $61/GB-month is ~2,700× the price of S3 Standard storage. It's a latency product, not a storage product, and sizing a 10% hot set at 100M ops (11.4 GB) costs **$702/mo** — nearly 10× the entire Express One Zone bill it was meant to accelerate. Don't put the reuse store in Redis. If you want a miss-avoidance layer, a Bloom filter in process memory does the same job for free.

### As a percentage of model spend

The denominator has to be a baseline that already has provider prefix caching on and tuned, so I built per-call costs with caching applied. Anthropic list prices (Opus 5 $5/$25 per MTok, Sonnet 5 $3/$15, Haiku 4.5 $1/$5; cache reads ~0.1×, writes 1.25× at 5-minute TTL and 2× at 1-hour) — **these I took from the bundled `claude-api` skill's cached table rather than fetching [platform.claude.com/docs/en/pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/pricing) live, so treat them as one step removed from source.**

- Heavy turn (Opus 5, 40k in @ 90% cached, 2k out): **$0.088/call**
- Mid turn (Sonnet 5, 20k in @ 85% cached, 1k out): **$0.029/call**
- Cheap call (Haiku 4.5, 8k in @ 80% cached, 400 out): **$0.0042/call**

Because both storage cost and model spend scale linearly in operations, the ratio is **flat across all three volume tiers** — 10k and 100M give the same percentage. What moves it is the mix:

| Workload mix | S3 Standard | Express One Zone | R2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Every op is a heavy Opus 5 call | 0.002% | 0.0008% | 0.002% |
| Every op is a mid Sonnet 5 call | 0.007% | 0.003% | 0.006% |
| 1 model call per 3 ops, mid | 0.023% | 0.008% | 0.018% |
| 1 model call per 10 ops, cheap Haiku | 0.51% | 0.18% | 0.41% |

The worst realistic case is about **half a percent** of model spend, and the typical agentic case is **two to twenty basis points**. The one exception is the 10k-ops tier *if you attach managed infrastructure*: a $47/mo RDS index against 10k cheap Haiku calls ($42/mo of model spend) is **112% of model spend** — the store costs more than the models. That's a floor problem, not a storage problem, and it disappears if you use content-addressed object keys and skip the index.

### What this means for the premise

The break-even is the number worth carrying: at 100M ops on S3 Standard the store costs $2.17 per million operations, and a single avoided mid-tier model call is worth $0.029. **One hit per ~13,400 operations pays for the entire store.** On the cheap-Haiku profile it's one hit per ~1,950. Any hit rate you'd plausibly bother measuring is orders of magnitude above break-even.

So storage cost cannot be the thing that decides whether this system is worth building — it's noise against model spend at every scale I priced. Which means the objection to the design, if there is one, has to live somewhere else: in whether the reuse key can be computed correctly and cheaply (hashing every input artifact on every operation is CPU you haven't costed), in how far the invalidation cascade propagates when an ancestor changes, and in whether the hits actually materialize once you've subtracted everything provider prefix caching already gets for free. That last one is the real contest, and it isn't a cost question at all.

### Bottom line

- **Storage is 1–9% of the "storage" bill; requests are 70–90%.** At 100M ops/month on S3 Standard: $2.63 storage, $190 requests, $24 egress. Optimize request pricing, not storage class.
- **Total cost: ~$0.02/mo at 10k ops, ~$2/mo at 1M, ~$217/mo at 100M** on S3 Standard, 4 KB objects, 70% hit rate, 30-day retention. S3 Express One Zone cuts the 100M case to **$74**; Cloudflare R2 to **$173** with zero egress.
- **As a share of model spend: 0.002% to 0.5%**, flat across all three volume tiers, worst case being cheap Haiku calls with many tool operations per model call. Typical agentic workload: **0.02–0.2%**.
- **Never use S3 IA / One Zone-IA / Glacier IR.** The 128 KB minimum billable object size makes 4 KB objects cost 32× their bytes — Standard-IA's effective $0.40/GB-mo is 17× *worse* than S3 Standard.
- **Retention is nearly free.** 30 days → 12 months costs +13% total ($217 → $246). Buy the long window.
- **Don't put it in Redis.** ElastiCache Serverless Valkey is $61.32/GB-month, ~2,700× S3; a 10% hot set at 100M ops is $702/mo, ~10× the whole object-store bill.
- **The small tier is a floor problem.** At 10k ops the marginal cost is $0.02, but a managed index (RDS t4g.medium, $47.45/mo) is 112% of model spend for cheap calls. Use the content hash as the object key and carry no index — a miss is just a 404 GET.
- **Break-even is one hit per ~13,400 operations** (mid-tier model calls). Cost is not what decides this design; hit rate against an already-prefix-cached baseline is.

# Staleness cost by domain

## The reframe: the unit of analysis is the operation, not the domain

The premise of the question — "which domains tolerate a nonzero staleness rate" — is one level too coarse. In the reuse-key model, staleness has exactly one cause: **a real input to the operation that is not in the hash**. If every determinant of the result is in the key, the stored answer is not stale, it is correct by construction, forever. Staleness is therefore a measure of *hidden input churn*, and hidden input churn splits each of the six domains along the same seam:

- **Extraction from a fixed artifact.** "What is the total on this PDF?", "Where is the change-of-control clause in this executed contract?", "What procedure is documented in this signed encounter note?" The artifact is immutable and content-hashed. Absent a model or schema change — both of which *are* in the key — the correct answer never changes. Staleness ≈ 0 by construction, in every one of the six domains including the regulated ones.
- **Judgment against a mutable external corpus.** "Is this dependency vulnerable?", "Is this code bundle billable under current NCCI edits?", "Is this claim payable under the current policy and state regulation?" The corpus (CVE/KEV feeds, ICD-10-CM/CPT, payer LCD/NCD policy, fee schedules, case law) is a real input that a naive key omits. Staleness ∝ corpus churn rate.

That distinction cuts across all six domains and matters more than the domain label. Below, costs first; then the tolerance arithmetic that follows from them.

## What a wrong answer costs, by domain

**Code review and CI triage.** The lowest-severity domain, and it is not close. A false positive costs an engineer's attention; a false negative costs an escaped defect. The macro anchor is CISQ's estimate that poor software quality cost the US economy **$2.41 trillion in 2022**, of which **$1.52 trillion** is accumulated technical debt ([CISQ/Synopsys, Dec 2022](https://news.synopsys.com/2022-12-06-Software-Quality-Issues-in-the-U-S-Cost-an-Estimated-2-41-Trillion-in-2022)). Per-incident, the ceiling is downtime: ITIC's surveys report that **over 90% of mid-size and large enterprises put one hour of unplanned downtime at $300,000 or more**, with 41% of large enterprises at $1M–$5M/hour ([ITIC 2024](https://itic-corp.com/itic-2024-hourly-cost-of-downtime-report/); [ITIC 2025-26 via Lenovo](https://www.lenovo.com/content/dam/lenovo/dcg/global/en/products/servers/itic-2025-global-server-hardware-reliability-survey-results.pdf)). The critical structural fact is that this domain is *saturated with independent downstream checks*: compilation, tests, CI, a human approver, staged rollout, and DORA's change-failure-rate feedback loop. The noise floor is already high — Google's own data has ~16% of its 4.2M tests exhibiting some flakiness, and flaky-test overhead is routinely put at double-digit percentages of developer time (widely cited from Google's engineering productivity work; treat the specific percentages as secondary-sourced). A stale review comment lands in a channel that already emits mostly-ignorable output.

**Security vulnerability triage.** Severely asymmetric. False positives are free because they are already the norm — the Oxford/USENIX study is literally titled ["99% False Positives: A Qualitative Study of SOC Analysts' Perspectives on Security Alarms"](https://www.usenix.org/conference/usenixsecurity22/presentation/alahmadi) (Alahmadi, Axon & Martinovic, USENIX Security 2022), and commercial SAST false-positive rates are commonly quoted at 40–60% (vendor sources; weak evidence, treat as directional). False negatives have no downstream check at all — the next event is exploitation. IBM's [Cost of a Data Breach 2025](https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach) puts the global average at **$4.44M** (down 9% from $4.88M), with **healthcare at $7.42M** ([HIPAA Journal summary](https://www.hipaajournal.com/average-cost-of-a-healthcare-data-breach-2025/)), and Verizon's [2025 DBIR](https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/2025-dbir-data-breach-investigations-report.pdf) found vulnerability exploitation was the initial access vector in **20% of breaches, up 34% year over year**. This is also the domain with the fastest hidden-input churn: the CVE/KEV/EPSS corpus changes daily, so "this is not exploitable" has a genuinely short half-life while the code it describes has not changed at all.

**Invoice and financial data extraction.** Moderate severity, and — this is the important part — near-zero intrinsic staleness, because the invoice is an immutable artifact. The cost of a wrong extraction is an overpayment or a duplicate: industry benchmarks put duplicate payments at roughly **0.1–0.5% of AP spend**, with recovery audits clawing back only **0.05–0.5% of audited spend** (secondary/vendor benchmarks; directional only). Regulatory exposure exists but is small per item: IRS §6721 penalties for incorrect information returns run **$60 / $130 / $340 per return** depending on lateness for tax year 2026, and **$680 per return for intentional disregard with no maximum** ([IRS](https://www.irs.gov/payments/information-return-penalties)). The "no maximum for intentional disregard" clause matters below.

**Medical coding.** High severity, two-sided, with long detection latency and per-claim statutory penalties. Undercoding costs revenue; overcoding creates False Claims Act exposure. Current FCA civil penalties are **$14,308 to $28,619 per claim** for violations assessed after July 3, 2025 ([28 C.F.R. § 85.5](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/28/85.5)) — *per claim*, and on top of **treble damages**. DOJ recovered **over $6.8 billion** in FCA settlements and judgments in FY2025, **over $5.7 billion of it health care**, from a record **1,297 qui tam suits** ([DOJ, Jan 2026](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/false-claims-act-settlements-and-judgments-exceed-68b-fiscal-year-2025)). HIPAA adds a separate per-violation layer: **$145 to $2,190,294** under the 2026 inflation adjustment effective Jan 28, 2026 ([Mercer](https://www.mercer.com/insights/law-and-policy/hhs-adjusts-2026-hipaa-certain-aca-and-msp-monetary-penalties/)). Ordinary rework, by contrast, is cheap: MGMA benchmarks the cost to rework a denied claim at **$25.20**, Premier measured **$43.84 (2022)** and **$57.23 (2023)**, with a full published range of roughly $25–$181. The gap between $57 of rework and $28,619 + treble is the entire risk story. Note also that the human baseline is not clean: CMS's FY2025 Medicare fee-for-service **improper payment rate was 6.55%, or $28.83 billion** ([CMS CERT](https://www.cms.gov/data-research/monitoring-programs/improper-payment-measurement-programs/comprehensive-error-rate-testing-cert)), and the industry's own accuracy benchmark is **95%** — i.e., a 5% error rate is the professional standard ([AHIMA journal](https://journal.ahima.org/)).

**Insurance claims.** Two-sided like coding, with a regulatory floor on the underpay side. Overpayment shows up as claims leakage, put at **5–10% of total claims payments** across P&C in commonly-cited industry analysis (attributed to McKinsey; secondary sourcing, treat as a range not a measurement). Underpayment triggers the NAIC Unfair Claims Settlement Practices model act as adopted by states, market-conduct exam findings, and common-law bad faith — where the exposure is extracontractual and can exceed policy limits by orders of magnitude. Both directions are checked, but by different adversaries on different clocks.

**Legal clause extraction.** The lowest per-item cost and the highest tail. WorldCC's benchmark — still the standard cite — puts average **contract value erosion at 9.2% of contract value** from poor contract and commercial management, with top performers holding leakage to ~3% ([WorldCC](https://www.worldcc.com/Portals/IACCM/Resources/10655_0_Overcoming-the-10-pitfalls.pdf); provenance confirmed by [Deloitte](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/services/tax/articles/contract-management-lifecycle-insights.html)). A missed indemnity cap or change-of-control provision in M&A diligence is discovered by an adversary years later, in litigation, with no intervening check. But — again — clause *location and text* extraction from an executed contract is immutable; only clause *interpretation* under changing law is not.

## Which domains tolerate a nonzero staleness rate

The tolerance condition is `p · q · C < b`, where `p` = probability the stored answer is materially stale, `q` = probability a stale answer escapes downstream detection, `C` = cost per escaped error, and `b` = savings per reused operation. Against a baseline that already has provider prefix caching on, `b` is small — the marginal saving is the ~10% cached-input rate you'd still have paid plus the full output tokens, realistically **$0.01–$0.05 per reused model call**. That small `b` is what makes the arithmetic bite.

Working the numbers (my `C` and `q` figures are estimates, clearly flagged; the resulting `p` thresholds are arithmetic from them):

| Domain | Est. C per escaped error | Est. q (escape rate) | Max tolerable p |
|---|---|---|---|
| Code review / CI triage | ~$500 | ~0.05 (CI + tests + human approver) | **~1.6 × 10⁻³** |
| Invoice extraction | ~$5,000 | ~0.5 (three-way match catches some) | ~1.6 × 10⁻⁵ *(but p≈0 structurally)* |
| Legal clause extraction | ~$50,000 tail-weighted | ~0.9 (no intervening check) | ~1 × 10⁻⁶ *(but p≈0 for extraction)* |
| Insurance claims | ~$2,000 | ~0.4 (two adversarial checks) | ~5 × 10⁻⁵ |
| Medical coding (overcode direction) | ~$1,000+ expected FCA-weighted | ~0.5 (payer adjudication misses overcoding — that *is* the 6.55%) | ~1 × 10⁻⁴ |
| Security triage (false-negative direction) | ~$4,400 (0.1% of a $4.44M breach) | ~1.0 (nothing checks a dismissed alert) | **~1 × 10⁻⁵** |

Read the table by comparing the two columns that aren't estimates. Code review tolerates a stale rate roughly **two orders of magnitude higher** than anything else, entirely because of `q`, not because of `C`. And the domains where `p` is structurally near zero — invoice extraction, legal clause extraction — pass despite punishing thresholds, because the artifact cannot change.

Two consequences follow that I'd put weight on:

**Error direction dominates error rate.** Security triage has essentially unlimited tolerance for one answer ("escalate to a human") and essentially zero for its complement ("not exploitable"). A reuse layer that serves stored results *only in the safe direction* and always recomputes the unsafe one is admissible in domains that are otherwise closed. This is a design choice available today and it converts security triage from unaddressable to addressable at the cost of roughly half the hit rate. The same asymmetry exists in coding (undercode is safe, overcode is not) and claims (paying is safe, denying is not).

**In regulated domains, the provenance chain is worth more than the tokens.** A content-addressed store that can prove *exactly which artifact hashes, model id, and rule-corpus version produced this coded claim* is a compliance artifact — it is the documentation an FCA defense or a market-conduct exam actually wants. Given how small `b` is against a prefix-cached baseline, that is the more defensible thing to sell into medical coding, claims, and legal.

## The opposite case: consistency as a product — and its trap

The variance-reduction argument is real and the evidence for it is stronger than the evidence for most of the cost figures above. Kahneman's noise audit at a large insurer found the **median pairwise difference between two underwriters pricing the same policy was 55%**, and **43–44% between two claims adjusters on identical claims**, against executive expectations of ~10% ([*Chance*/Taylor & Francis](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09332480.2024.2416879); [strategy+business](https://www.strategy-business.com/article/How-noisy-is-your-company); original: [Kahneman et al., HBR 2016](https://hbr.org/2016/10/noise)). In eDiscovery, Roitblat, Kershaw & Oot (2010) found two independent human review teams achieved only **49% and 54% recall** on the same corpus. In radiology, subspecialist second interpretations change recommended management in ~26% of studies. Medical coding's own professional standard concedes a 5% error rate.

So in exactly the high-value domains, the incumbent is not "correct" — it is noisy. A stored good result has zero variance across servings. If the stored answer's error rate sits below the fresh-recompute variance, reuse improves expected quality rather than merely cutting cost, and inconsistency is itself the compliance failure in claims handling (disparate treatment of like claims) and in coding audits.

**But reuse converts random error into systematic error, and that is strictly worse in every domain with a per-item statutory penalty.** A noisy human process makes uncorrelated errors that partially wash out at portfolio level. A cached wrong answer makes the *same* error ten thousand times. At $14,308–$28,619 per claim plus treble damages, or $680 per information return with no maximum, the tail is what kills you, and correlated errors have a far heavier tail at identical mean error rate. Worse, the legal character of the error changes: a scattered set of coder mistakes is negligence, while a reproducible, systematic, repeated miscoding is the fact pattern that supports **knowledge or reckless disregard** — the scienter element of the FCA — and supports applying a multiplier across the entire affected population rather than a sampled subset. Sell "we reduce your decision variance" into a per-item-penalty domain and you are selling a benefit whose price is paid entirely in the tail.

The clean version of the consistency pitch survives only where the penalty is not per item: code review and CI triage (consistent findings across a monorepo), and portfolio-level contract review where the value is comparability across 400 agreements rather than correctness of any one.

## Bottom line

- **Staleness is not a domain property; it is a measure of inputs missing from the hash.** Extraction from an immutable artifact — invoices, executed contracts, signed clinical notes — has `p ≈ 0` by construction and is safe to reuse *even in the most regulated domains*. Judgment against a mutable corpus (CVE feeds, ICD-10/CPT, payer policy, fee schedules) is where staleness lives. Every one of the six domains contains both.
- **Only code review and CI triage tolerate a meaningful stale rate** (est. ~10⁻³, roughly 100× everything else) — and the reason is `q`, not `C`. Tests, CI, and a human approver are independent downstream checks; the channel is already dominated by ignorable output.
- **Security triage is the worst fit on the merits and the best fit on structure.** False positives are already 99% of the volume and cost nothing; false negatives have zero downstream detection and a $4.44M average consequence. Perfectly asymmetric, so a direction-aware policy (reuse only "escalate", always recompute "clear") makes it addressable.
- **Medical coding, claims, and legal are addressable at the extraction layer and closed at the judgment layer.** The separator is per-item statutory penalties: FCA at **$14,308–$28,619 per claim plus treble damages**, HIPAA to **$2,190,294**, IRS §6721 with **no maximum for intentional disregard**.
- **Consistency is a genuine product** — the human baseline is 55%/43% pairwise variance (insurance), 49–54% recall (eDiscovery), 95% accuracy-by-standard (coding) — **but reuse turns noise into bias.** Correlated errors have a heavier tail than uncorrelated ones at equal mean rate, and a reproducible systematic error is the fact pattern that establishes FCA scienter. Pitch variance reduction in code review and portfolio-level contract comparability; do not pitch it into per-claim penalty regimes.
- **Given how thin `b` is against a prefix-cached baseline** (~$0.01–$0.05 per reused call), the defensible product in regulated domains is the **provenance chain, not the token savings** — a store that can prove which artifact hashes, model id, and rule-corpus version produced a given output is the audit evidence those buyers actually want.

## Cold-share: what fraction of real agent traffic arrives after the provider cache has expired

### What "cold" actually means, mechanically

The threshold is **idle time, not age**. Anthropic's docs state the 5-minute TTL "is refreshed for no additional cost each time the cached content is used," and the lifetime "is measured from the start of the request that writes or reads the cache entry, not from the end of its response." OpenAI's is the same shape — for GPT-5.6+ a 30-minute TTL where "the lifetime begins when the prefix is written and refreshes whenever the prefix is reused," and for earlier models "5 to 10 minutes of inactivity, up to a maximum of one hour," with an extended-retention option up to 24 hours. So a continuously-exercised prefix never goes cold, at any traffic level. Cold share is a function of **throughput per distinct prefix**, not of calendar schedule — which is why the answer differs by two orders of magnitude across the four patterns below.

Three other mechanics bound the comparison. Reads cost 0.1×, writes 1.25× (5m) or 2.0× (1h), so the money at stake in a cold arrival is the write premium, not the full input price. Minimum cacheable length is 512–4,096 tokens depending on model, so short operations were never cacheable either way. And caches are "isolated between organizations… also isolated per workspace within an organization" — a reuse layer spanning tenants has a scope advantage the provider cache structurally cannot match, though it also inherits the privacy problem that isolation exists to solve.

### Measured: interactive coding agent

I measured this end-to-end rather than estimating it. Harness: `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-jamesyang-Documents-GitHub-Brevitas-Systems/30a08619-bfdd-4d15-a8c6-1c8b59d5d979/scratchpad/coldshare2.py` and `.../tokweight.py`, read-only over 3,090 Claude Code transcripts (183 top-level sessions plus subagent threads) spanning 2026-07-20 → 2026-08-17, 28.1 days. After deduplicating on `requestId` and `tool_use.id` (transcripts double-record resumed sessions — the un-deduplicated run overstated cross-session repeats by ~80%): **49,581 billed requests, 6,523,964,543 prompt tokens, 69,432 tool invocations.** These are Anthropic's own usage counters, not estimates.

Realized mix: **96.45% of prompt tokens billed at the 0.1× read rate**, 3.53% cache writes, 0.018% fresh input. Against a no-cache counterfactual at Sonnet-class list price that is an 85.3% saving — consistent with the only published field figure I could find, arXiv 2607.13080 (Peng, Lin & Lee, *Inference Economics of Enterprise Coding Agents*, July 2026), which reports "prompt caching (99.3% hit rate) cuts realized API cost by 88.6%."

Intra-session idle gaps: **median 3.1s, p90 21.2s, p99 390s. P(gap > 5m) = 1.12%, P(gap > 1h) = 0.21%.** Token-weighted, requests arriving after >1h idle are 0.21% of requests and **0.36% of prompt tokens** — but they carry **9.64% of all cache-write tokens**, and their read-to-prompt ratio collapses to 6.1% versus 96.9% for hot arrivals. That collapse is the cold signature, and it is cleanly visible in the data, which is what makes the 0.36% credible rather than an artifact of the classifier.

The exclusive-value ceiling follows arithmetically. If a perfect layer converted every >1h-cold write (22.2 Mtok) into a read, it recovers **3.08% of the input bill**. That is the ceiling for a warming layer, and it is an upper bound — it assumes zero warming cost, which prior work in this repo measured as net-negative against the 1h tier.

The reuse store's ceiling is much lower, because cold share is the *second* multiplier and the first one is tiny. Hashing each model call's full preceding message chain (a proxy for the exact prefix a reuse key would cover): **only 0.62% of model calls have an exactly-repeated prefix**, because agent conversations grow monotonically — every turn is a novel full prompt even though it shares a long prefix. Of those repeats, 22.2% are cold at the 1h tier. Exclusive addressable share: **0.137% of calls**. Tool invocations do better on repeat rate — **5.21% repeat** (3,615 of 69,432), of which **30.3% are cold at 1h** and 15.4% are >24h — for an exclusive share of **1.58% of tool ops**. Per tool the spread is wide and interpretable: `Read` repeats 34.8% of the time (44.5% cold at 1h — file re-reads across sessions); `WebFetch` repeats 0.86% and **0% of those are cold at 1h** (the provider TTL already covers every re-fetch); `WebSearch` repeats 0.61% but 69.6% cold.

Two sub-populations behave very differently, and this is where the commercial argument actually lives:

- **Cross-session repeats are 85.0% cold at 1h** (54.5% are >24h), versus 9.6% for same-session repeats. Cross-session is 27% of the repeat population. Cross-project session-open gaps: median 314s, **30.9% cold at 1h, 50.8% cold at 5m**. Session-first requests still read 40.5% of their prefix from cache, so cross-session sharing is real — it is just worth little, because a session's first request is one of many.
- **7.6% of tool repeats occur <1s apart.** These are concurrent duplicates from parallel subagents. The provider cache definitionally cannot serve them — Anthropic's docs say "a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins," and this repo's own live probe (X1, 2026-08-14) found five callers at 0ms skew all billed `cache_creation`, zero reads. A reuse store with in-flight deduplication beats the provider cache here **regardless of TTL**. This is the one structural, non-TTL advantage in the whole dataset.

**Caveat, stated plainly:** one user, one harness. The arrival distribution is not claimed to generalize, and no invoice has been reconciled — every dollar is rate-card arithmetic over vendor-reported counters.

### Measured: per-commit CI

Measured live against the GitHub REST API on 2026-08-17 (`.../ci_cadence.py`, `.../midtail.py`), because published CI-cadence figures are scarce and stale.

Eight of the busiest repos in open source, last 100 default-branch commits: inter-commit **median 184s (rust-lang/rust) to 4,509s (kubernetes/kubernetes)**; cold at 1h ranges **16% to 58%**, cold at 5m **47% to 88%**. Gaps between consecutive runs of the *same* workflow are much tighter — cold at 1h was 0–6% for six of the eight (next.js 0%, pytorch 0%, rust 1%, vscode 2%, home-assistant 4%, airflow 6%), 32% for langchain, and 84% for kubernetes whose sampled workflows are sparse and span 148 days.

A mid-tail sample (19 repos, 100–1,000 stars, pushed within the last week): median-of-medians inter-commit gap **1,204s**, mean cold at 1h **29.6%**, mean cold at 5m **75.9%**. Note several of those repos are bot-driven with a near-exact 3,600s cadence, which lands pathologically on the 1h boundary.

**Estimate, flagged as such:** both samples are biased toward active repos — a repo that pushed today is active by construction. A typical enterprise service repo at a handful of commits per day has inter-commit gaps of hours, so **~90–100% of its CI runs arrive cold at any TTL**. But the token-weighted picture inverts: within one CI run, if N jobs share a prefix, only the first is cold, so **cold token share ≈ 1/N**. For a matrix build with 20–200 jobs that is 0.5–5%.

### Estimated: nightly batch and monthly close

These need no measurement, only arithmetic, and the arithmetic is the interesting part.

**Nightly batch:** run-to-run gap is 24h, which exceeds every TTL on the market except OpenAI's extended 24h retention, where it sits exactly on the boundary. So **100% of cross-run reuse is cold**. But within a run, N items share the prefix and only the first pays. At N = 10³–10⁵ (the realistic range for a nightly job), **cold token share is 0.001%–0.1%**. Nightly batch is the pattern that *sounds* maximally favorable to a reuse layer and is in fact the least favorable, because all the tokens live in the hot within-run population. Anthropic's Batch API compounds this: batches mostly complete within an hour and carry a 50% discount independently.

**Monthly close:** ~30d cycle gap → **100% cold across cycles**, same 1/N within. The difference is that N is small — tens to low hundreds of calls — so **cold token share lands around 1–10%**. Monthly close has the highest cold *token* share of the four patterns and the lowest absolute volume, which is the whole problem in miniature.

**Chat agents** (estimate, grounded in BurstGPT — arXiv 2401.17644, Wang et al., 10.31M traces over 213 days of Azure OpenAI): "over 35% of conversations end with only one request," with a "median of 2 and 75% of conversations with four or fewer requests." Single-request conversations have zero within-conversation reuse. The reusable asset is the shared system prompt across concurrent users, and at any real traffic level that prefix is exercised far more often than every 5 minutes, so its cold share is ≈0. Per-user conversation history is the opposite — a user returning hours later is always cold. I'd put the token-weighted cold share for chat at **20–50%, wide band, assumed not measured**, because the split depends entirely on the history-to-system-prompt token ratio, which I have no production data for.

For an upper bound on how much reuse exists at all: Mooncake (arXiv 2407.00079, Kimi production) reports that "up to only 50% of the KVCache can be reused in our current workloads, even if we assume both the capacity of storage and the TTFT SLO are infinite," with hit ratio rising 30%→50% as capacity grows 1k→50k blocks, and "over 50% of cache blocks remaining unused." Infinite capacity and infinite TTL — i.e. a perfect reuse store — caps out at 50% on a real long-context workload.

### The structural result

Cold share and reuse rate are **anti-correlated by construction**. Anything with enough throughput to generate many repeats keeps its own cache warm; anything cold enough to defeat the provider cache doesn't repeat often enough to matter. Every pattern I measured or derived sits on that curve, and the product of the two multipliers — repeat rate × cold share — never exceeded 1.6% of operations in real traffic.

## Bottom line

- **Interactive coding agent (measured, 6.52B prompt tokens / 28 days):** cold arrivals are **0.21% of requests and 0.36% of prompt tokens** at the 1h tier (1.12% of requests at 5m). Ceiling on recoverable spend from a perfect warm-everything layer: **3.08% of the input bill**. Ceiling from an exact-key reuse store: **0.137%**.
- **Per-commit CI (measured live via GitHub API):** **16–58% cold at 1h** on the eight busiest OSS repos, **29.6% mean** on a mid-tail sample; ~90–100% for a typical low-activity enterprise repo *(estimated)*. But cold **token** share is ~1/N of a matrix build — 0.5–5%.
- **Nightly batch (arithmetic):** 100% cold across runs, **0.001–0.1% cold by token volume** within a run. The pattern that sounds best for a reuse layer is the worst.
- **Monthly close (arithmetic):** 100% cold across cycles, **~1–10% by token volume**. Highest cold share, lowest absolute volume.
- **Chat agents (estimated from BurstGPT):** shared system prompt ≈0% cold at any real traffic; per-user history mostly cold. Band **20–50%**, not measured.
- **Cold share is the second multiplier, not the first.** Exact-repeat rate is **0.62% for model calls** (agent prefixes grow monotonically, so almost every prompt is novel) and **5.21% for tool calls**. Exclusive addressable share = repeat × cold = **0.137% / 1.58%** of operations.
- **The one structural win is concurrency, not TTL.** 7.6% of tool repeats arrive <1s apart; Anthropic's docs confirm "a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins," and our live probe showed 5-way simultaneous fan-out billing 5 writes and 0 reads. In-flight deduplication beats the provider cache there at any TTL — that is a stronger commercial story than cold share, and it is the one worth building on.
- **Cross-tenant scope is the second structural gap:** "caches are isolated between organizations… also isolated per workspace." A shared store spans that boundary — and inherits the privacy problem it exists to enforce.
- **Verify before quoting:** 5m TTL refreshes free on every use (Anthropic); OpenAI is 30m refreshing on GPT-5.6+, 5–10m idle/1h max on older, up to 24h with extended retention; minimum cacheable prefix 512–4,096 tokens varies non-monotonically by model.
