## Measured end-to-end cost reductions

**The one controlled academic measurement.** "Don't Break the Cache: An Evaluation of Prompt Caching for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks" (Lumer et al., PwC; arXiv 2601.06007, submitted 2026-01-09, revised 2026-01-31) is the closest thing to a proper experiment. Methodology: DeepResearch Bench, 100 PhD-level research tasks, a 10,000-token system prompt, agents doing autonomous web-search tool calls; 40 independent sessions per cache condition across 4 cache modes and 4 models (~640 sessions). Cost computed from `cached`/`cache_creation`/standard token counts in API responses times list pricing. Critically, **the baseline prepends a UUID to the system prompt to deliberately break the cache** — so their numbers measure the *total* value of provider caching versus a forcibly-uncached world, not incremental value over a default configuration.

Best cache mode per model: GPT-5.2 **79.6%** cost reduction (excluding tool results from the cached region; range across modes 79.3–81.4%), Claude Sonnet 4.5 **78.5%** (77.8–78.5%), GPT-4o **45.9%** (45.9–47.8%), Gemini 2.5 Pro **41.4%** (27.8–41.4%). TTFT improved 13–31%. The paper reports **no cache hit rates** — only cost and latency deltas. It also found naive full-context caching can regress latency (GPT-4o full-context: −8.8% TTFT) because dynamic tool results trigger cache writes for content never reused.

**First-party production instrumentation.** Three teams published their own spend:

- **ProjectDiscovery** (`how-we-cut-llm-cost-with-prompt-caching`), on their security agent Neo, measurement window 2026-02-02 to 2026-03-30, 9.8B tokens served from cache. Hit rate went **7% → 84%** (85% in the final 10 days); cost fell **59%** overall, 66% post-optimization, 70% in the last 10 days. Their stated method is the right one: *"These figures come from actual reported costs, not estimated pricing — we derive the effective per-token rate from real spend, then compare it against what that same volume would have cost if every input token was charged at the standard rate."* One extreme task: 67.5M input tokens over 1,225 steps at 91.8% cache rate versus 3.2% pre-optimization. Note this is a **before/after of their own misconfiguration**, not caching-vs-no-caching — caching was nominally "on" the whole time at 7%.
- **Deriv** (2026-07-23), production assistant "Amy" on GPT-5: **85.8% hit rate → 77% input-token cost reduction**, computed per-request as cached ÷ total input tokens tracked over time. Traffic volume withheld; the dollar figures in the post are illustrative extrapolations onto 30B tokens/month.
- **LangChain** (`deep-agents-prompt-caching`), their own Deep Agents eval suite on real agent trajectories, cost deltas pulled from LangSmith traces: **Claude Haiku 4.5 −77%, GPT-5.4-mini −80%, Gemini 3.5-Flash −49%**. No hit rates published.

**Independent probe of OpenAI's automatic cache** (HN 46070749, ~8 months ago): a network-monitoring chatbot, 10 tools, ~1,400-token prefix, logging `cached_tokens` on every response across gpt-4o-mini/gpt-5-mini/gpt-5. Result: **80–90% hit rates after the first call, 47–49% reduction on input tokens** — the gap between hit rate and savings being the 50% (4o-mini) vs 90% (gpt-5 family) cached-input discount. This author also observed cross-model cache sharing within the family.

**A measured ceiling on the discount itself.** "Cache-Aware Prompt Compression" (Yan Song, arXiv 2607.15516, 2026-07-17) characterized Anthropic Sonnet 4.6's cache empirically and found it is *not* the ρ=1.0 ideal the literature assumes: a two-tier architecture with a sharp threshold near 3,500 tokens, below which **the hit rate plateaus at ρ≈0.83 across 30-call sessions**. On an enterprise tool-using assistant with a 94k-token schema prefix, caching alone gave 51.7% cost reduction at compression ratio 3; their compression layer added a mean 49% *on top of* cache-only.

Google states it *"automatically passes on cost savings"* for implicit caching with **no percentage at all**.

## What this means for the denominator

Three facts compound against anyone trying to sell caching savings. First, **it's on by default on two of three major providers**: OpenAI caches automatically above 1,024 tokens with no code change, and Gemini implicit caching is enabled by default for 2.5+ models (4,096-token minimum on 3.x Flash / 3.1 Pro). Anthropic requires explicit `cache_control`, but Claude Code and the Agent SDK insert it for you. Second, **shipped agent harnesses already sit at 89–93%** (Galileo's Claude Code and Codex measurements), which leaves at most single-digit percentage points of prefix to recover. Third, **after caching works, cache reads become the bill**: Martin Alderson's modeling (2026-08-10, explicitly a constructed scenario, not instrumented) puts cache reads at 76.4% of total cost for a 100-turn Opus 5 session and 81.6% for GPT-5.6 — about $0.5 per GB-hour of context, versus well under a cent per GB-hour for AWS RAM. The residual opportunity is not "turn caching on"; it's the cost of the reads themselves and the workloads where the prefix is structurally unstable.

## Bottom line

- **Established (multiple independent instruments agree).** Provider-native prompt caching alone, versus a forcibly-uncached baseline, cuts end-to-end agent API cost by roughly **40–80%**, converging near **75–80% on frontier Anthropic and OpenAI models** and **~41–50% on Gemini and older/cheaper-discount models**. Sources: arXiv 2601.06007 (640 sessions, controlled), LangChain (own eval suite, 49–80%), ProjectDiscovery (own production spend, 59–70%), Deriv (own production, 77%), HN independent probe (47–49% on OpenAI). The spread across models is explained almost entirely by the provider's cached-read discount, not by workload.
- **Established.** Well-structured production agent loops run at **85–93% cache hit rates** (Galileo: Claude Code 92.7%, Codex 89.6%; ProjectDiscovery 84–85%; Deriv 85.8%; independent OpenAI probe 80–90%). Whatever value provider caching contains is therefore *already realized* in mainstream harnesses, and a third party's addressable share of that 40–80% is the residual few points, not the headline.
- **Established.** Caching is default-on at OpenAI (automatic ≥1,024 tokens) and Google (implicit, ≥2,048–4,096 tokens), and auto-inserted by Anthropic's own agent tooling. No customer action, and therefore no vendor, is required to capture the bulk of it.
- **Established.** The savings are not monotone in effort. Naive full-context caching regressed TTFT by 8.8% on GPT-4o (arXiv 2601.06007), and marking never-reused content costs write premium — consistent with your own ROI-gate finding.
- **Contested.** Baseline hit rates for *unoptimized* agents. ProjectDiscovery's 7% is one real, well-documented case of caching being nominally on and effectively off, and essentially the entire "your hit rate is probably 7%" content genre traces back to that single data point. Galileo's OpenClaw operator at 23.8% is a second independent low reading. Against that, DeepSeek's fleet-wide 56.3% and OpenRouter's provider-level 75–87% suggest the population is far better than 7%. There is no defensible published estimate of the distribution.
- **Contested.** Whether the discount is actually 0.1× in practice. arXiv 2607.15516 measured Sonnet 4.6's hit rate plateauing at **ρ≈0.83** below a ~3,500-token threshold, meaning realized savings fall materially short of the pricing-sheet ceiling — a two-tier structure no other source has replicated or refuted.
- **Contested.** Whether cross-session and cross-machine caching contributes anything at scale. Claude Code's docs state the cache is effectively scoped to one machine and directory (working dir, platform, git snapshot all sit in the prefix), while the underlying API cache is org-wide — but nobody has published measured cross-user hit rates.
- **Unknown.** No provider publishes aggregate hit rates or the fraction of billed input tokens served from cache. Anthropic explicitly runs on this metric internally (SEVs when it drops) and has published no number. DeepSeek's 56.3% from Feb 2025 is the only fleet-wide figure in existence, and it predates the agent era.
- **Unknown.** The dollar-weighted denominator — what share of *total industry agent spend* currently flows through a cache hit. Every measurement above is per-session or per-customer; none aggregates to spend. Without that, "how much is left to sell" cannot be sized from published data.
- **Unknown / no evidence found.** I found **zero** published measurements of incremental savings from a third-party caching layer over an already-correctly-configured provider cache on a real workload. The only quantified "on top of" results are research prototypes measured against their own baselines: CAPC (+49% over cache-only, LongBench-v2 and synthetic workloads) and TokenPilot (arXiv 2606.17016, 56–87% vs prior systems), neither validated on production spend. That gap is the load-bearing absence for the commercial question.

## LLM gateway & caching market survey — as of 2026-08-17

**Method note first, because it bounds everything below.** The WebSearch budget for this session was already exhausted when I started, so this is built entirely from direct fetches of vendor docs and pricing pages that I navigated to by known URL. That means good fidelity on the vendors I checked and *no discovery layer* — a stealth or newly-launched product doing dependency-aware reuse would not surface here. Treat the negative finding at the end as "absent from twelve vendors' live docs," not "proven not to exist."

### The category split that matters

Two unrelated things are both sold as "caching," and conflating them is the main source of noise in this market:

1. **Gateway response cache** — the gateway stores the full response and replays it, so the provider call never happens. Savings are 100% of the request on a hit. Matching is either exact (hash of the request) or semantic (embedding similarity).
2. **Provider prefix-cache pass-through** — the gateway forwards or injects `cache_control` breakpoints and the *provider* discounts input tokens. Anthropic prices this at 1.25× base input for a 5-minute write, 2× for a 1-hour write, and 0.1× for reads ([Anthropic prompt caching docs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)). The call still happens; only input tokens get cheaper.

Nobody I found sells a third thing.

### Vendor by vendor

**Portkey.** Simple (exact) cache on the free Developer tier with 1-day TTL; semantic cache advertised on the $49/mo Production tier ([pricing](https://portkey.ai/pricing)). Production is 100k recorded logs/mo with $9 per additional 100k; Enterprise is custom at 10M+ logs. Simple-cache keys hash the full request body plus `x-portkey-metadata` headers plus an optional `x-portkey-cache-namespace`; TTL runs 60s to 90 days, default 7 days. Semantic mode does exact first, then cosine search at a 0.95 default threshold, ignoring system prompts. Invalidation is TTL plus a `cache_force_refresh` header — nothing dependency-aware ([cache docs](https://portkey.ai/docs/product/ai-gateway/cache-simple-and-semantic)). **Contested within their own site:** the pricing page lists "Simple & Semantic Caching" on the $49 tier, while the docs page says semantic "requires a vector database and is only available on select Enterprise plans." Their savings claim is "up to 20x faster and cheaper" — a vendor claim with no methodology attached.

**Helicone.** Exact match only, explicitly: keys hash URL, full body, relevant headers, and an optional cache seed, and "any change in these components creates a new cache entry" ([caching docs](https://docs.helicone.ai/features/advanced-usage/caching)). Stored in Cloudflare Workers KV, default `max-age=604800` (7 days), max 365 days. Unusual feature: bucket size up to 20, where the same request randomly returns one of N stored responses. Their gateway passes provider cache-control through via the `@helicone/helpers` SDK rather than injecting it ([gateway prompt-caching page](https://docs.helicone.ai/gateway/concepts/prompt-caching)). Pricing: Hobby free (10k req/mo, 7-day retention), Pro $79/mo, Team $799/mo, Enterprise custom, all with "usage-based pricing applies" on top ([pricing](https://www.helicone.ai/pricing)). The per-log overage rate is not published — the page only offers a calculator. Docs make no numeric savings claim.

**LiteLLM.** The widest backend matrix: in-memory, disk, Redis, S3, GCS, plus three semantic backends (Qdrant, Redis-semantic, Valkey). Keys hash the full request; `x-litellm-cache-key` exposes them; per-request `no-cache`, `no-store`, `ttl`, `s-maxage`, `namespace`. Invalidation is TTL plus a manual `/cache/delete` — no dependency tracking ([caching docs](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/caching)).

The most interesting artifact in this entire survey is on that page, and it cuts *against* LiteLLM's own feature: **"Semantic caching is designed for single-shot prompts. On multi-turn or agentic traffic it will replay stale responses."** The explanation is that consecutive turns append to a nearly identical message array, so embedding similarity produces false hits — typically showing up as an agent repeating the same tool call — and raising the threshold does not reliably fix it. They recommend exact-match Redis for agentic traffic instead. I verified this verbatim on a second fetch specifically to rule out summarizer invention. This is a vendor documenting a negative result about a category everyone else markets without caveat.

LiteLLM also auto-injects Anthropic `cache_control` as of v1.94.0, opt-in via `enable_anthropic_prompt_caching` or `LITELLM_ENABLE_ANTHROPIC_PROMPT_CACHING`, placing one checkpoint on the system prompt and one on the trailing turn, standing down if the client supplied its own, and respecting Anthropic's 4-block limit ([prompt caching tutorial](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/tutorials/prompt_caching)). That page carries a "reduce costs by up to 90%" claim — vendor claim, unqualified. Pricing: OSS free self-hosted; Enterprise is a custom annual quote "sized to your annual gateway request capacity, deployment architecture, and support needs — never per token" ([pricing](https://www.litellm.ai/pricing)). No dollar figure is published.

**Cloudflare AI Gateway.** Exact match only, and unambiguous about it: "caching is based on exact match of the entire request. Any difference in the body — including messages, tools, or model parameters — will result in a separate cache entry." Key is SHA-256 over provider + endpoint + model + provider auth header + full body, overridable with `cf-aig-cache-key`. TTL 60s to one month. Semantic is explicitly future work: "We plan on adding semantic search for caching in the future" ([caching docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/features/caching/)). Caching itself is free — analytics, caching, and rate limiting all are; you pay for logs (100k total on Workers Free, 10M per gateway on Workers Paid), Logpush beyond 10M req/mo at $0.05/million, and a 5% fee on unified-billing credit purchases with provider rates passed through at no markup ([pricing](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/reference/pricing/)). The [2026 changelog](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/changelog/) shows the recent investment going into billing unification (2026-08-07) and identity-aware spend controls (2026-08-05), not caching.

**Kong AI Gateway.** The `ai-semantic-cache` plugin does both semantic and exact modes, backed by Redis VSS / Redis Cloud / Valkey 3.14+ / pgvector, or managed ElastiCache, Azure Managed Redis, Memorystore. Notably candid caveat: "when Exact Caching is enabled, the AI Semantic Cache plugin may still return results for queries that are similar but not identical." Respects `max-age` / `s-maxage`; no invalidation or dependency features documented. **Enterprise-only, Kong Gateway 3.8+** ([plugin docs](https://developer.konghq.com/plugins/ai-semantic-cache/)). Konnect Plus includes 1M API requests/mo with $200/mo per additional 1M, and 5 unique LLM models with $100/mo per additional model ([pricing](https://konghq.com/pricing)).

**OpenRouter.** Ships **no response cache of its own**. It is a pass-through plus a routing optimizer: after a cached request it remembers which provider served you and pins subsequent requests there to keep the provider's cache warm, with `session_id` usable as an explicit sticky key that activates "even before cache usage is observed" ([prompt caching docs](https://openrouter.ai/docs/features/prompt-caching)). Anthropic still requires caller-supplied `cache_control` (either one top-level field that auto-places the breakpoint at the last cacheable block, or per-block); OpenAI, DeepSeek, and Grok are automatic provider-side. OpenRouter takes **no margin on cached tokens** and no inference markup; it monetizes credit purchases at 5.5% via Stripe ($0.80 minimum) or 5% via crypto, plus a 5% BYOK fee above $25,000/mo on pay-as-you-go or $200,000/mo on Enterprise ([FAQ](https://openrouter.ai/docs/faq)).

**Braintrust.** The AI proxy caches exact-match on `/chat/completions`, `/embeddings`, `/moderations`, and in default `auto` mode caches only when `temperature=0` or a `seed` is set — a deliberately conservative correctness posture nobody else matches. Default TTL one week, `x-bt-cache-ttl` from 1 to 604,800s, and the cache is AES-GCM encrypted under a key derived from your API key so "Braintrust cannot see your data" ([proxy docs](https://www.braintrust.dev/docs/guides/proxy)). Notably, Braintrust makes **no cost-savings claim at all** — the only vendor here that doesn't. Pricing is eval-shaped, not gateway-shaped: Starter $0 with $10 model credits, 1GB, 10k scores, 14-day retention; Pro $249/mo with $249 credits, 5GB then $3/GB, 50k scores then $1.50/1k, 30-day retention; Enterprise custom ([pricing](https://www.braintrust.dev/pricing)).

**Vercel AI Gateway.** No response caching feature exists in the product — the [overview](https://vercel.com/docs/ai-gateway) (last updated 2026-07-28) lists routing, fallbacks, embeddings, spend monitoring, and zero markup, with no cache. Pricing is zero markup and zero platform fee on tokens including BYOK; the add-ons that do cost money are Custom Reporting ($0.075 per 1,000 tag/user/quota writes, $5 per 1,000 reporting queries), team-wide provider allowlist ($0.10 per 1,000 successful requests), and team-wide ZDR ($0.10 per 1,000 requests) ([pricing](https://vercel.com/docs/ai-gateway/pricing), last updated 2026-08-01).

**TrueFoundry.** Exact-match plus semantic via an `x-tfy-cache-config` header with `type`, `similarity_threshold` (guidance: start at 0.9), `ttl`, and `namespace`. Their semantic implementation embeds *only the last message* while requiring all other parameters to match exactly, and they frame it as "Semantic cache is a superset of exact-match cache." They also draw the cleanest version of the category distinction above: gateway cache hits "bypass LLM providers entirely… a significant advantage over provider-level prompt caching, which only reduces token processing costs" ([caching docs](https://www.truefoundry.com/docs/gateway/caching)). Pricing: Developer $0 (50k req/mo, 3 users), Pro $499/mo (1M req/mo, 10 users, +$499 for 2M req and 5 API keys), Pro Plus $2,999/mo (1M req/mo, 25 users), Enterprise custom at 10M+ ([pricing](https://www.truefoundry.com/pricing)).

**Others.** Requesty is 5% markup pay-as-you-go with a free tier of 200 req/day on free models, and states "Routing, caching and EU data residency are included on every plan" — but all three of its caching doc paths I tried 404'd, so the cache *type* is unverified ([pricing](https://requesty.ai/pricing)). Bifrost (Maxim) is Apache 2.0 and ships semantic caching, with enterprise features unpriced publicly ([repo](https://github.com/maximhq/bifrost)). GPTCache (Zilliz) remains the OSS reference implementation of exact + semantic with LRU/FIFO/LFU/RR eviction and no dependency-aware invalidation; I could not confirm its current maintenance status from the repo page and would not rely on it ([repo](https://github.com/zilliztech/GPTCache)).

### Does anyone ship cross-run dependency-tracked reuse?

No — not in any of the twelve products above.

Every cache surveyed keys on one of exactly two things: a hash of the request bytes, or an embedding of the last user message. Every invalidation mechanism surveyed is one of exactly two things: TTL expiry, or a manual bypass/purge (`cache_force_refresh`, `no-cache`/`no-store` + `/cache/delete`, `cf-aig-cache-key`). Not one vendor doc mentions recording what a cached output *depended on*, or invalidating an entry because an upstream input changed.

Three things get close enough to be worth naming so they aren't mistaken for it:

- **Namespaces and cache seeds** (Portkey `x-portkey-cache-namespace`, Helicone cache seed, LiteLLM `namespace`, TrueFoundry `namespace`). These partition a keyspace. Partitioning is not dependency tracking — it tells the cache who may share an entry, never why an entry is still valid.
- **OpenRouter sticky routing / `session_id`.** This *is* genuine cross-run reuse — it deliberately keeps a provider prefix cache warm across separate requests — but the validity test is byte-prefix equality within the provider's TTL. Nothing is tracked.
- **Anthropic's automatic advancing breakpoint.** Same shape: cross-request reuse within TTL, purely prefix equality, provider-side.

The structural reason for the gap is visible in LiteLLM's warning. The industry's answer to "make caches hit more often" was semantic similarity, and semantic similarity is precisely the technique that breaks on the traffic that has grown fastest — multi-turn and agentic. A vendor now documents that failure in its own product docs and steers agentic users back to exact match. That leaves the market with exact match (safe, low hit rate on agentic traffic) and prefix pass-through (provider-priced, 0.1× reads, TTL-bounded), and nothing in between.

### Bottom line

**Established (from live pricing/docs pages, not inference):**
- Gateway-level response caching is universally exact-match-or-semantic and universally TTL-invalidated. Confirmed exact-only: Cloudflare, Helicone, Braintrust. Semantic offered: Portkey (Enterprise per docs), Kong (Enterprise-only), LiteLLM, TrueFoundry, Bifrost, GPTCache. No response cache at all: OpenRouter, Vercel.
- Caching is not a revenue line anywhere. Cloudflare gives it away free; Vercel and OpenRouter take zero markup on tokens and monetize credits (5% / 5.5%) or add-ons; the rest bundle it into observability seats and log volume ($49–$799/mo Portkey/Helicone, $499–$2,999/mo TrueFoundry, $249/mo Braintrust, $200/mo per extra 1M requests at Kong). Nobody prices against savings delivered.
- Semantic caching is consistently gated to the highest tier where it exists — Kong Enterprise-only, Portkey "select Enterprise plans."
- Provider prefix-cache pass-through is table stakes; auto-injection is not. LiteLLM auto-injects Anthropic breakpoints behind an opt-in flag (v1.94.0+). OpenRouter, Portkey, and Helicone all require caller-supplied `cache_control` for Anthropic.
- **Nobody ships dependency-tracked reuse.** Zero of twelve vendor doc sets mention dependency tracking or upstream-change invalidation.

**Contested:**

- Whether semantic caching is safe on agentic traffic at all. LiteLLM says flatly it is not and will "replay stale responses"; Kong concedes its exact mode "may still return results for queries that are similar but not identical"; Portkey, TrueFoundry, and Bifrost market it with no such caveat. Braintrust's `temperature=0`-or-`seed` gate is a fourth, stricter position on the same question.

**Unknown:**

# Response-level caching for LLMs: what the evidence actually shows

**Method note first, because it bounds everything below.** This session's web-search budget was exhausted before I started, so I worked from direct fetches: the arXiv API (which functions as a decent literature search), the GitHub API for issues and repo state, and vendor documentation pages fetched live today (2026-08-17). That is good coverage of papers, vendor docs, and bug trackers, and poor coverage of blog posts and conference talks. Where I say "I found no published post-mortem," read it as "none in papers, HN, or the major gateways' issue trackers" — not as an exhaustive claim. A few figures below come from a summarizer reading paper full-text rather than from my own reading of the tables; I flag those.

## The three things people call "caching" are not the same

Provider-side **prompt caching** (Anthropic, and the equivalents elsewhere) is a *prefix* match over the rendered request bytes — it reuses computation for a shared prefix and re-runs generation every time. It cannot serve a wrong answer, because it never reuses an answer. **Exact-match response caching** hashes the whole request and replays the stored response; its correctness risk is limited to staleness. **Semantic response caching** embeds the prompt, does an ANN lookup, and replays a stored answer when a neighbor is within a threshold. Only the third one can be wrong about *which* answer, and essentially all the interesting evidence concerns it.

Worth noting where the market actually landed: [Cloudflare AI Gateway](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/features/caching/) is exact-match only — SHA-256 over provider, endpoint, model, auth header, and full request body, with "We plan on adding semantic search for caching in the future" — and [Helicone](https://docs.helicone.ai/features/advanced-usage/caching) is likewise exact-match only. The two most widely deployed gateway/observability products declined to ship the semantic version.

## Reported hit rates, and on what traffic

**Vendor claims, unaccompanied by methodology or accuracy figures.** [Redis LangCache](https://redis.io/langcache/) headlines "Save 90% on API costs" and cites a customer (Mangoes.ai) at a 70% hit rate, 70% LLM-spend savings, and 4× faster responses. There is no false-positive rate, no precision/recall, and no description of how similarity thresholds were set. [Portkey](https://portkey.ai/docs/product/ai-gateway/cache-simple-and-semantic) claims "up to 20x faster and cheaper" and documents a default cosine threshold of 0.95, with no accuracy metrics and no discussion of wrong answers anywhere on the page.

**Measured results, mostly academic.** The single most useful paper is [vCache: Verified Semantic Prompt Caching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03771) (v5, Feb 2026; ICLR 2026), because it benchmarks the *static-threshold* design that GPTCache and every gateway implement. On SemCacheLMArena (60,000 real LM-Arena prompts, `text-embedding-3-small` + GPT-4o-mini), a GPTCache-style static threshold of 0.98 yields ~53% hit rate at a 4.1% error rate; tightening to 0.99 drops it to ~37% hit at 2.5% error. On 150,000 web-search queries at 0.99, error reaches 1.7% after 150k samples — and error *grows with corpus size*, since more cached neighbors means more chances for a spurious near-match. vCache's own learned per-entry thresholds hit the user-specified bound (0.5% error at 41% hit; 2.0% at 54% hit). Correctness was labeled by string matching for classification and by LLM-as-judge for open-ended prompts. (These specific table values came via a full-text summarizer pass, not my own reading of the PDF; the abstract's headline claims — "up to 12.5× higher cache hit and 26× lower error rates" versus static-threshold and fine-tuned-embedding baselines — I verified directly.)

Hit rate is overwhelmingly a function of traffic shape, not of cache quality. A [category-aware position paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26835) (Oct 2025) reports 40–60% for high-repetition categories like code versus 5–15% for conversational or volatile ones, and notes the economics: remote vector search puts break-even at a 15–20% hit rate, which is why 20–30% of production traffic goes uncached. Other points on the curve: a production NL-to-code system reports [67% hit rate at 94.3% "semantic accuracy"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11687) over 10,000+ queries — i.e., roughly 1 in 17 hits wrong, with no stated validation methodology; an [ensemble-embedding approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07061) reports 92% hit on Quora Question Pairs with 85% accuracy at *rejecting* non-equivalents, i.e. a 15% false-accept rate on negatives (and QQP is a paraphrase benchmark, not traffic); and [generative caching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17565) claims 83% with "minimal incorrect hits," unquantified.

The one clean "zero false hits" result is [semantic caching for OLAP via LLM query canonicalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.19811): 82% hit rate versus 28% (text) and 56% (AST) across 1,395 TPC-DS/SSB/NYC-TLC queries, with zero false hits — achieved by requiring "exact intent matches under strict schema validation and confidence-gated NL acceptance." That is the tell. Zero false hits is attainable exactly where equivalence is *decidable*, which is not the case for free-form prompts.

## How the "slightly different prompt" problem is handled

Four mechanisms, in descending order of how common they are and ascending order of how well they work.

**A similarity threshold, tuned by the operator.** This is the whole answer in most products, and the vendors' own recommended settings amount to admitting it doesn't generalize. Microsoft's [`llm-semantic-cache-lookup` policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/api-management/azure-openai-semantic-cache-lookup-policy) requires `score-threshold` with no default, and advises: "Start with a low value such as 0.05 and adjust... Score threshold above 0.2 may lead to cache mismatch. Consider using lower value for sensitive use cases." Since lower means *stricter* there, Microsoft's recommended operating point is effectively near-duplicate matching. The same page carries the frankest vendor statement I found anywhere: "Because semantic caching returns responses based on similarity (not exact match), it can surface responses that are incorrect, outdated, or unsafe for the current request. Evaluate this feature carefully for your workload and include safeguards."

**Scope restriction and partitioning.** Portkey tries exact match first and only runs semantic search on a miss, and limits semantic caching to requests under 8,191 tokens with ≤4 messages. Azure offers `vary-by` (recommended for cross-user isolation), `ignore-system-messages` (recommended `true`), and `max-message-count` to stop caching deep in a dialogue. On the LiteLLM side, per-team scoping and multi-tenant isolation are still open feature requests ([#29955](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/29955), [#19575](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/19575)) — so cross-tenant cache reuse is a live concern, not a solved one.

**Verification of the hit.** The strongest signal that thresholds alone are insufficient is that the reference implementation gave up on them: GPTCache's final commit (2025-07-11, PR #669) added "a new post-processing type for verifying hit questions using LLM." [Krites](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13165) moves that judge off the critical path — asynchronously LLM-judging borderline neighbors and promoting verified pairs — reporting up to 3.9× more requests served from curated answers, though on *trace-driven simulation*, not production. [LaCache](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01718) validates the first k speculatively decoded tokens rather than the prompt alone. The economic tension is obvious: a judge that is itself an LLM call eats the savings the cache exists to produce.

**Learned per-request thresholds with an error bound** (vCache) — the only approach that turns "how wrong will this be?" into a parameter you set rather than a property you discover.

## Measured false-hit rates, and how correctness gets validated

Consolidating: **2.5–4.1%** on open-ended chat at GPTCache-style thresholds, **~1.7%** on search queries at a very tight 0.99, an implied **~5.7%** in one production code-gen deployment, **15%** false-accept on QQP negatives, **0%** in a domain with decidable equivalence. Validation is LLM-as-judge for open-ended output and string/schema equality for classification and SQL. **No gateway vendor publishes a false-hit rate at all** — not Portkey, not Redis LangCache, not Kong, not Azure.

There is also a deeper measurement problem. ["Closing the Calibration Gap in Semantic Caching"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19719) (v2, June 2026) evaluates on LangCache SentencePairs v3 (74,265 pairs, 45% positive) and introduces P-CHR AUC — precision across cache-utilization levels — because standard PR-AUC measures ranking while deployment runs at a fixed threshold. Reported P-CHR AUC: 0.402 for ColBERTv2.0, 0.353/0.330 for MNRL rerankers, 0.199/0.173 for BCE rerankers, 0.385 for the average retriever baseline. Models retain only **23–42%** of their offline ranking quality once deployed, and the paper decomposes the gap into a recoverable calibration term (0.28–0.43) and a structural, irreducible term (~0.19 at a 45% positive rate) that post-hoc calibration cannot close. In plain terms: the embedding-model benchmark numbers vendors cite systematically overstate the precision you get in production.

## Post-mortems

**I found no published production post-mortem of a semantic cache serving wrong answers.** HN's archive (via Algolia) contains tool launches, one Ask HN worrying that "correctness risk seems to make most of these approaches scary in practice," and a founder observation that "semantic caches we tried didn't have a sense of context" — but no incident write-up. That absence is itself informative, and it cuts two ways: either the failures are rare, or they are invisible, since a false hit returns a fluent, plausible answer with a 200 and no error signal. Given the calibration-gap result, invisibility is the better bet.

The closest public artifacts are bug reports, and they are instructive.

[LiteLLM #12234](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/12234) (July 2025, closed stale October 2025): with `redis-semantic` at `similarity_threshold: 0.8`, the prompts "Hello world," "What is 1+1?", "How's the weather today?", and "What is artificial intelligence?" *all* returned the same cached greeting. A commenter later diagnosed it: the parameter behaves as a **distance** threshold, not a similarity one, so 0.8 accepted everything within distance 0.8 — an inverted-polarity config that fails open into a ~100% false-hit rate, silently, with no error.

The mirror image is [LiteLLM #29086](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/29086): a tenant-isolation change made `_get_cache_key_filter_expression` return a RediSearch tag filter scoped to the **full SHA-256 request hash**, which runs as a pre-filter *before* KNN. Any non-byte-identical prompt produced an empty candidate set, so "the KNN similarity search never executes. The distance threshold is never evaluated." Semantic caching silently degraded to exact matching from v1.85.1 through at least v1.86.2, closed June 2026 — and [#31610](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/31610) reports the same symptom still open on v1.90.0. The evidentiary implication matters more than the bug: a deployment can report "semantic caching enabled" while doing neither semantic matching nor any measurement of whether it works.

LiteLLM's [live caching docs](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/caching) now carry the sharpest vendor warning I found — a documented failure mode rather than a disclaimer. Semantic caching "is designed for single-shot prompts. On multi-turn or agentic traffic it will replay stale responses," because "consecutive turns are nearly identical text and their embeddings are ~0.99 similar. At any practical threshold, every turn matches the previous turn's cached entry and the client replays a stale response, which typically shows up as an agent repeating the same tool call over and over." A related open issue ([#28778](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/28778)) reports tool-return JSON being lost on agent traffic under both `redis-semantic` and `qdrant-semantic`. Kong documents its own version of the surprise: with exact caching enabled, "the AI Semantic Cache plugin may still return results for queries that are similar but not identical. This is expected behavior."

Adversarially, the picture is worse. [CacheAttack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.23088) (v2, Jan 2026; ICML 2026) is an automated black-box collision attack achieving **"a hit rate of 86% in LLM response hijacking,"** transferable across embedding models, and it names the structural reason no threshold fixes this: "the locality required to maximize cache hit rates fundamentally conflicts with the cryptographic avalanche effect necessary for collision resistance." LaCache is the defense response.

Finally, on the reference implementation itself: [GPTCache](https://github.com/zilliztech/GPTCache) is at 8,156 stars, last release v0.1.44 in **August 2024**, last commit **2025-07-11**. Not archived, but ~13 months dormant as of today. Its [own paper](https://aclanthology.org/2023.nlposs-1.24/) (Bang, NLP-OSS 2023) reports exactly one number — "2-10 times" faster on a hit — and no hit rate, precision, or error rate at all.

## Bottom line

**Established:**
- Semantic caching's error rate is real, measurable, and non-trivial on open-ended traffic: **2.5–4.1% wrong answers at 37–53% hit rate** on 60k real chat prompts at GPTCache-style thresholds (vCache, ICLR 2026), and error grows with cache size.
- Hit rate is a property of traffic, not of the cache: **40–60% for code-like repetitive workloads, 5–15% for conversational**, with remote-vector-search economics putting break-even around 15–20%.
- Offline embedding benchmarks overstate deployed precision. Rerankers retain only **23–42%** of offline ranking quality at real thresholds, and roughly 0.19 of the gap is structurally irreducible.
- Vendors handle the different-prompt-different-answer problem almost entirely with an operator-tuned threshold, and their own recommended settings (Azure: start at 0.05, above 0.2 "may lead to cache mismatch") amount to near-duplicate matching. Azure states plainly that the feature "can surface responses that are incorrect, outdated, or unsafe."
- Multi-turn and agentic traffic is a documented failure mode, not an edge case: consecutive turns embed at ~0.99 similarity, so at any practical threshold each turn matches the previous one and replays a stale response — LiteLLM's own docs describe the resulting agent tool-call loop.
- Zero-false-hit semantic caching is achievable only where equivalence is decidable (SQL over a known schema: 82% hit, zero false hits). It is not achievable for free-form prompts.
- Semantic caches are attackable: 86% response-hijack success in a published black-box collision attack, with a stated structural tension between hit-rate locality and collision resistance.
- The reference open-source implementation (GPTCache) is effectively unmaintained, and its own paper publishes no hit-rate or accuracy figures.

**Contested / weakly supported:**
- Vendor hit-rate and savings claims (Redis LangCache's 70%/90%, Portkey's "20x") — single customer anecdotes or unqualified headlines, with no methodology and, in every case I checked, **no accuracy figure whatsoever**.
- Whether verification-on-hit (LLM judge, speculative-token check) pays for itself. Krites reports up to 3.9× more curated-answer coverage, but from trace-driven simulation, not production, and a judge call erodes the savings.
- Whether reported semantic hit rates from gateway deployments are even measuring semantic matching. LiteLLM's `redis-semantic` silently degraded to exact matching for roughly a year, with no error raised; the current version still has open reports of the same symptom.
- The one production-deployment accuracy figure I found (67% hit, 94.3% accuracy over 10,000+ queries) states no validation methodology in the abstract.

**Unknown:**
- **The production false-hit rate of any commercially deployed semantic cache.** No vendor publishes one. Every figure above is from an academic benchmark.
- Whether false hits are actually rare in production or merely undetected. A false hit is a fluent answer with a 200 status and no error signal, and the calibration-gap result argues for undetected.
- Whether any public post-mortem of a semantic cache serving wrong answers exists. I found none in the arXiv literature, HN's archive, or the major gateways' issue trackers — but my search excluded general web/blog sources, so treat this as an unresolved gap rather than a negative finding.
- How LLM-as-judge labeling error propagates into the reported error rates. Every open-ended benchmark here relies on it, and none I read quantify the judge's own accuracy.

# KV-Cache Reuse Systems: What Is Reused, Against What Baseline

**Verification note.** Web search quota for this session was exhausted before I began, so every claim below comes from a direct fetch of a primary source (arXiv full text, vendor docs, vendor blogs, or GitHub source) performed today, 2026-08-17. Where a fetch summarizer produced a number I could not find in the source text, I extracted the PDF locally and say so explicitly.

---

## vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching (APC)

**What is reused:** KV blocks for exact token-prefix matches. vLLM V1 hashes full blocks only, chaining parent-block hash + block token IDs + extra keys (LoRA ID, multimodal input hash) so blocks are unique per model/adapter context. Partial blocks are never cached.

**Scope:** Single engine instance, GPU-resident, request-to-request. Cross-node sharing requires an external connector (LMCache, Mooncake, NIXL) — vLLM itself is node-local. The Mooncake paper states this directly: *"Similar reuse logic is already implemented in vLLM, but the open-source version of vLLM only supports local KVCache caching."*

**Reported saving:** vLLM publishes **no headline speedup number** for APC. Its docs instead state limits: APC *"only reduces the time of processing the queries (the prefilling phase) and does not reduce the time of generating new tokens,"* so there is no gain when decode dominates or when prefixes are not shared. This is unusually honest for the category.

**Default status — a live documentation error worth flagging.** `docs/features/automatic_prefix_caching.md` on `main` today still reads *"Set `enable_prefix_caching=True` in vLLM engine to enable APC."* But `vllm/config/cache.py` on `main` reads `enable_prefix_caching: bool = True`. **APC is on by default** and the docs are stale. This matters enormously for reading everyone else's benchmarks: any 2025+ comparison "against vLLM" that does not state its flags most likely had prefix caching *on*, while any 2023–24 comparison had it *off* (the first `enable_prefix_caching` commits in vLLM date to March 2024).

**Independent measurement — the only genuinely third-party one I found.** Zine et al., *"Attention to Detail: Evaluating Energy, Performance, and Accuracy Trade-offs Across vLLM Configurations"* (arXiv 2607.09172, Jul 2026), ran ~9,000 runs / 93,600 measurements over 5 open-weight models on A100-40GB. With FlashAttention-3, enabling prefix caching **improved latency in 37 of 50 model-task combinations and TTFT in 38 of 50** — and *increased* energy for Llama-3B on one task. Their characterization: *"small task-dependent optimization rather than uniform benefit."* No academic or vendor source I found reports APC-vs-no-APC as a large uniform win.

## SGLang RadixAttention

**What is reused:** KV cache of shared token prefixes across requests, held in an LRU radix tree, plus a cache-aware scheduler. The paper proves DFS visit order yields the optimal hit rate for a batch given cache size ≥ max request length.

**Scope:** Request-to-request within one engine. The paper also benchmarks a *"weakly consistent distributed cache"* across four workers on MMLU, reporting linear scaling.

**Reported saving:** *"up to 6.4× higher throughput"* and *"reduces latency by up to 3.7×"* (arXiv 2312.07104 v2, NeurIPS'24). Measured cache hit rates *"range from 50% to 99%"* across benchmarks, and the scheduler *"approaches 96% of the optimal hit rate on average."*

**Baseline — this is the critical finding.** The paper states: *"We use vLLM v0.2.5 and its default API server,"* alongside Guidance v0.1.8 (llama.cpp) and LMQL v0.7.3 (HF Transformers). vLLM v0.2.5 shipped in December 2023, **months before APC existed**. The authors say so explicitly: *"RadixAttention has been partially integrated as an optional experimental feature into the latest version of vLLM; therefore, we used an earlier version for comparison."* The 6.4× is measured against a **non-caching baseline, by deliberate construction**, and the authors disclose it. Anyone citing 6.4× as the value of RadixAttention *over today's vLLM* is misreading the paper.

The paper also contains its own negative result, which almost never travels with the headline: *"For long outputs, because there is not much sharing between different chat sessions and the decoding time dominates, there is almost no speedup."* The 6.4× maximum landed on MMLU — few-shot prompting, where the shared prefix is nearly the entire input.

---

## SGLang HiCache (the current production form of RadixAttention)

**What is reused:** Same prefix KV, extended down a memory hierarchy. HiRadixTree nodes record *where* each span lives — L1 GPU, L2 host DRAM, or L3 distributed store — and query L3 metadata live rather than synchronizing it.

**Scope:** *"L1 and L2 KV caches are private to each inference instance, whereas the L3 KV cache is shared among all inference instances within the cluster."* L3 backends: Mooncake, DeepSeek 3FS, NIXL, AIBrix KVCache, or LMCache. This is the clearest articulation of scope in the field. A newer `--enable-session-radix-cache` adds session-scoped eviction preference, with the honest caveat that session references are *"soft protection, not memory pins."*

**Reported saving and baseline:** Here the baseline **is** an already-caching system (SGLang with GPU-only RadixAttention), which makes these the more informative numbers. The LMSYS blog (2025-09-10) claims *"up to 6× throughput improvement and up to 80% reduction in TTFT"* from internal benchmarks — but publishes no tables, so treat as vendor claim. The operator-reported figures are more useful:

- **Novita AI**, Qwen3-Coder-480B, coding-agent workload, 25K+ token dialogues, ~8 turns: *"average TTFT dropped by 56%, inference throughput doubled, and the cache hit rate jumped from 40% to 80%."* This is a genuine over-an-already-caching-system measurement.
- **Ant Group**, DeepSeek-R1-671B, PD-disaggregated: *"84% reduction in TTFT compared to full re-computation"* — note the baseline silently reverts to no-cache here.

## LMCache (with CacheGen and CacheBlend)

**What is reused:** More than prefixes. LMCache stores and moves KV across requests, sessions, and *engine instances*; CacheBlend additionally fuses KV from **non-prefix, out-of-order text chunks** by selectively recomputing a small token subset. Tiers span GPU, CPU RAM, local SSD, Redis/Valkey, Mooncake, InfiniStore, S3-compatible object storage, NIXL, and GDS. Multi-node P2P CPU memory sharing is documented as moving from experimental to production in 2026/01. 11.2k GitHub stars.

**The papers (measured, peer-reviewed):**

- **CacheGen** (SIGCOMM'24, arXiv 2310.07240): *"3.5-4.3×"* KV size reduction and *"3.2-3.7×"* reduction in fetch-and-process delay. Baseline is other KV-reuse systems — but note this solves *transport*, not *reuse*, so it is not evidence that reuse itself pays.
- **CacheBlend** (arXiv 2405.16444 v3, Apr 2025; EuroSys'25): TTFT *"2.2–3.3×"* and throughput *"up to 5× compared with full KV recompute **and 3.3× compared with prefix caching**."* That second clause is one of the few clean, published, already-caching comparisons in the entire literature. Models: Mistral-7B, Yi-34B (8-bit), Llama-70B (8-bit); datasets 2WikiMQA, Musique, SAMSum, MultiNews. Quality cost: *"at most 0.015 loss in F1-score"* at 5–18% recomputation ratios, and it beats full KV reuse (PromptCache) by 0.1–0.2 absolute F1.

**The vendor benchmarks (mixed quality — one excellent, two under-specified):**

- **Docs `long-doc-qa` benchmark**, Qwen3-8B, 10 GB KV volume: mean TTFT 757 ms → 185 ms (−75%), duration 23.47 s → 13.79 s (−41%). Baseline is *"vLLM alone"* and the docs **do not state whether APC was enabled**. Given vLLM's default is now `True`, it probably was — but unstated is unstated. No hardware disclosed.
- **"10× MoE" blog (2026-04-03)**, Qwen3-235B on 8×H100-80GB, vLLM 0.18.1 + LMCache 0.4.3-dev. The underlying numbers are TTFT 3.98 s → 0.29 s (~13×), p99 13.55 s → 1.30 s (~10×), decode throughput 9.8 → 37.5 tok/s (~4×). Baseline is vLLM's in-process KV offloading with 8-way data parallelism and fragmented per-process buffers; prefix-caching status unstated. **The "10×" in the title is the p99 tail number** — not the mean and not the throughput number, which is 4×. This is headline-shopping across three metrics.
- **AMD MI300X agentic benchmark (2026-05-12) — the best-designed public benchmark I located, from any vendor.** Baseline explicitly launched with `--enable-prefix-caching`. MiniMax-M2.5 (230 GB FP8 MoE) on 2×MI300X (192 GB each), TP=2, replaying **739 anonymized Claude Code conversation traces** (median 60-min sessions, 93–97% prefix reuse across turns), 20 minutes at 32 concurrent users, 100k context:

| Metric | Vanilla | HBM Prefix Cache | LMCache |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requests completed | 18 | **12** | 28 |
| TTFT avg (s) | 150.84 | 102.17 | 34.59 |
| TTFT p95 (s) | 826.69 | 240.87 | 112.78 |
| Input throughput (tok/s) | 591 | **471** | 933 |

  Buried in the vendor's own data is the most interesting result on this page: **under memory pressure, enabling prefix caching alone was net-negative on throughput** — 12 requests vs 18, 471 tok/s vs 591 — while still cutting TTFT. Prefix caching bought latency by spending capacity. That is a real, measured, non-monotonic effect that no paper headline captures.

- **CacheBlend agentic post (2026-04-01)**, MTRAG Cloud corpus, 2 turns, prompt = system + query + retrieved doc. Prefix caching: TTFT 5.553 s → 4.055 s on turn 2, **48% hit rate**. CacheBlend: TTFT 2.325 s, **98% hit rate**. Net *"42% reduction in latency and 2× improvement in cache utilization"* over a prefix-caching baseline. Clean comparison; small workload.

## Mooncake

**What is reused:** Paged KVCache blocks identified by a chained prefix hash (their trace sample: *"the first 12 hash IDs are identical, indicating they can share prefix caching for the first 12*512 = 6,144 tokens"*), pooled in underutilized CPU DRAM and SSD across the cluster, with cache-aware **global scheduling** that selects a prefill instance on hit-length and block distribution rather than load alone.

**Scope:** Cluster-wide, explicitly positioned against vLLM's node-local caching. FAST'25 Best Paper. arXiv 2407.00079 v4 (Sep 3, 2025). Today Mooncake is also an L3 backend for SGLang HiCache, a vLLM connector, and an LMCache remote connector (6.3k stars); its Transfer Engine claims 87 GB/s on 4×200 Gbps RoCE and 190 GB/s on 8×400 Gbps, *"2.4x and 4.6x faster than TCP"* on 40 GB transfers.

**Reported saving vs baseline — the widest headline/reality gap in this survey.** The abstract's *"up to a 525% increase in throughput"* is against vLLM. Reading the evaluation:

- The full sentence is *"enhancements ranging from **50% to 525%**"* — 525% is the top of a wide range, not a typical value.
- The 525% comes from **simulated data** with engineered prompt lengths (16k–128k) and a **prescribed 50% cache-reuse ratio**, vLLM-[4M] as baseline. The paper concedes long-context simulated requests *"significantly disrupt the decoding stage of vLLM"* — so much of that gap is disaggregation, not caching.
- On **real public datasets**, the honest number appears: *"on the ArXiv Summarization and L-Eval datasets, Mooncake-[3P+1D] achieves throughput improvements of **20% and 40%**, respectively, over vLLM-[4M] while satisfying SLOs."* That is roughly one-fifteenth of the headline.
- The *"75% more requests"* figure is a real-trace replay (23,608 requests from a 1-hour production sample), Mooncake-[10P+10D] vs vLLM-[20M]. Crucially: *"The TTFT distributions for both... are nearly identical."* The win is entirely TBT SLO compliance (~100% vs 57%). **This is a disaggregation result, not a caching result.**
- Whether the vLLM baseline had prefix caching enabled is **never stated**.

**Ceiling on reuse, in their own words:** LRU on their trace, raising capacity from 1,000 to 50,000 blocks *"boosts the cache hit ratio from 30% to 50%"* — and *"Theoretically, up to only 50% of the KVCache can be reused in our current workloads, even if we assume both the capacity of storage and the TTFT SLO are infinite."*

**Number-laundering flag.** An automated summarization pass over the Mooncake PDF asserted a *"65% KVCache hit rate in production."* I extracted the full PDF text locally and regex-searched every sentence containing "hit rat|hit ratio|reuse rat|65%": **no such figure exists anywhere in the paper.** The real figures are 30%→50% and a 50% theoretical ceiling. Treat any citation of "Mooncake achieves 65% hit rate" as fabricated.

## Adjacent systems, briefly

- **Prompt Cache** (MLSys'24, arXiv 2311.04934) reuses attention states of *non-contiguous, position-independent* segments declared in a Prompt Markup Language schema. Claims 8× (GPU) to 60× (CPU) TTFT reduction — against **standard inference with no caching**, and it carries a real accuracy cost that CacheBlend later quantified (0.1–0.2 lower absolute F1 than selective recompute).
- **Preble** (arXiv 2407.00023 v2, Oct 2024) does distributed prompt-aware *scheduling*. Its baselines are **already-caching**: SGLang and vLLM-with-beta-prefix-sharing, each behind a round-robin balancer. Reports *"1.5×–14.5×"* avg and *"2×–10×"* p99 latency gains — but the range is workload-determined, and on the programming workload (longest decode) it collapses to *"1.56×–1.8× improvement in average latency."*
- **NVIDIA Dynamo** (7.8k stars, v1.0): KV-aware routing claimed at *"2x faster TTFT"* (Baseten, Qwen3-Coder 480B) and KVBM offloading GPU→CPU→SSD→remote. The *"7x throughput"* headline is *"DeepSeek R1 on GB200 NVL72 w/ Dynamo vs B200 without"* — **a hardware-generation change bundled into a software claim**. Unusable as evidence for KV reuse.
- **SwiftCache** (arXiv 2606.16135, Jun 2026) shares KV memory across *heterogeneous co-located models* over NVLink; baselines are vLLM and SGLang (already caching); *"P99 TTFT reduced by up to 69%."*

## The field's best data on how much reuse is actually left

**TraceLab** (arXiv 2606.30560, Jun 2026; Zhu, Jacob, Ma, Pan, Wang, Krishnamurthy, Kasikci) analyzed ~4,300 coding-agent sessions from 43 developers over ~8 months (Sep 2025–Jun 2026), spanning Claude Code and Codex across 20+ model versions — ~350,000 LLM steps and ~430,000 tool calls. Measured **provider-side prefix cache hit rates of 95.8% (Claude) and 95.7% (Codex)**, decomposing into tool-result steps at 97.9%/97.2% and user-initiated steps at only 86.9%/78.2%. Misses are driven by human idle time: *"when the gap is larger than 5 minutes, low-hit-rate steps begin to appear, and after 1 hour, almost all steps miss the cache."* Residual waste is real but bounded — *"fresh tokens are only 19.0% of append tokens,"* yielding *"prefill amplification by 5.3×"* overall (Claude 8.1×, Codex 3.9×), with human thinking time costing **12.8% of total API spend** via cache misses.

This is the single most decision-relevant measurement I found, because it establishes that on the workload everyone is optimizing for, the *deployed* baseline is already capturing ~96% of available prefix reuse. The remaining opportunity is concentrated in TTL-expiry on human-paced gaps, not in the reuse mechanism.

## Bottom line

**Established (measured, primary-source, reproducible):**

- vLLM APC defaults to **on** today (`vllm/config/cache.py`: `enable_prefix_caching: bool = True`), while vLLM's own docs still say you must enable it. Any post-2024 "vs vLLM" number without a stated flag is ambiguous.
- **SGLang's 6.4× is against a non-caching baseline by the authors' own explicit admission** (vLLM v0.2.5, pre-dating APC by months) and is a max on MMLU. The same paper reports *"almost no speedup"* on long-output multi-turn chat.
- **Mooncake's 525% is simulated data at a prescribed 50% reuse ratio**; on real public datasets the measured gain over vLLM is **20% and 40%**, and the real-trace "75% more requests" is a TBT/disaggregation win with *"nearly identical"* TTFT distributions.
- Mooncake's own trace analysis caps reuse at ~50%: *"only 50% of the KVCache can be reused in our current workloads, even if we assume both the capacity of storage and the TTFT SLO are infinite."*
- The genuinely clean over-an-already-caching comparisons are few and their numbers are modest: CacheBlend **3.3× throughput over prefix caching**; CacheBlend agentic **42% latency reduction, 48%→98% hit rate**; Novita/HiCache **TTFT −56%, hit rate 40%→80%**; Preble **1.56–1.8×** on its hardest workload.
- Under memory pressure on real agentic traces, LMCache's own MI300X benchmark shows **prefix caching alone was throughput-negative** (12 vs 18 requests, 471 vs 591 tok/s) while improving TTFT. Caching is not monotonically beneficial.
- On real coding-agent traffic, the deployed provider-side prefix cache already hits **95.7–95.8%**; residual prefill amplification is 5.3×, and human idle time costs **12.8% of spend**.
- The only large-N third-party evaluation of APC (93,600 measurements) finds it helps latency in **37/50** and TTFT in **38/50** model-task combinations — a task-dependent optimization, not a uniform win.

**Contested / unreliable as stated:**

- Every headline multiplier in this space — 6.4×, 525%, 10×, 14.5×, 7× — is the **maximum of a range on the most favorable workload**, and in three of five cases against a baseline with no caching at all. The medians, where disclosed, run 1.2×–2×.
- LMCache's "10×" is the p99 tail figure; the mean TTFT gain was 13× and the throughput gain 4×. Three metrics, headline drawn from whichever was largest.
- Dynamo's "7× throughput" compares GB200 NVL72 *with* Dynamo against B200 *without* — a hardware change reported as a software result. Not usable as evidence.
- **A "Mooncake 65% production hit rate" figure is circulating from automated summarization and does not exist in the paper.** Verified by local full-text extraction. The paper says 30%→50%.
- Whether prefix caching was enabled in the baseline arm is **unstated** in LMCache's docs benchmark, LMCache's MoE post, and Mooncake's entire evaluation. Only the LMCache MI300X post publishes the baseline launch command.

**Unknown:**

- No independent, non-vendor head-to-head of LMCache or HiCache against vLLM-with-APC-enabled exists in anything I could fetch. Every cross-node-vs-node-local comparison is published by a party shipping the cross-node layer.
- No published measurement isolates **how much of Mooncake's or Dynamo's gain is KV reuse versus prefill/decode disaggregation**, despite the two being bundled in every headline. Mooncake's own trace result (identical TTFT, better TBT) suggests the split favors disaggregation, but it is not decomposed.
- No public data on the marginal value of *cluster-scope* KV sharing over *node-local* prefix caching at a hit rate already in the 90s — which, per TraceLab, is where real agentic traffic sits. The 40%→80% Novita figure is the closest proxy and comes from a much lower starting point.
- LMSYS's *"up to 6× throughput, up to 80% TTFT reduction"* for HiCache is published without tables, hardware, or workload detail — vendor claim only.
- Quality/correctness costs of non-prefix reuse (CacheBlend, Prompt Cache, SemPIC-style position-independent caching) are measured only on short QA/summarization benchmarks. Nothing measures them on long-horizon agentic tool-calling, which is the workload the vendors now market to.

## Two axes, and why they separate cleanly

Every system in scope answers two independent questions: **what is the key** (a position in a program — step index, step id, node name, checkpoint id — versus a hash of the content flowing in), and **what is the reuse for** (getting a crashed run back to where it was, versus not paying twice for identical work). Almost every durable-execution engine answers "position" and "recovery." Almost every thing that answers "content" and "cost" is not a durable-execution engine — it's a cache layer or a data pipeline. The one interesting hybrid is LangGraph, which ships both mechanisms side by side with different keying, which is the cleanest natural experiment available.

Everything below is from primary docs fetched today (2026-08-17) or from source read at a pinned commit. Nothing here is a benchmark I ran; where a claim is vendor marketing rather than mechanism I say so.

## LangGraph — both mechanisms, in one library, keyed differently

**Durable replay is positional.** Source at `langchain-ai/langgraph@644815f` (release 1.2.11, 2026-08-11): a task's identity is `task_id_func(checkpoint_id_bytes, checkpoint_ns, str(step), name, PULL, *triggers)` (`libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/_algo.py:616-622`) — an xxh3 hash of checkpoint id, namespace, **step number**, node name, and trigger channels. No input content enters it. Completed work is recovered because its writes were persisted against that task id, not because anyone hashed what the node saw.

The docs are unusually explicit that this does *not* save money on the re-run portion: "Replay re-executes steps from a prior checkpoint… Nodes before the checkpoint are skipped (their results are already saved)" and "**Nodes after the checkpoint re-execute, including any LLM calls, API requests, or interrupts — which are always re-triggered during replay**" ([checkpointers](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/checkpointers.md)). Within a failed super-step there is a partial-credit mechanism: "When a graph node fails mid-execution at a given super-step, LangGraph stores pending checkpoint writes from any other nodes that completed successfully… When you resume graph execution from that super-step you don't re-run the successful nodes." Same page. That is crash recovery with a sibling-level granularity, keyed by task id.

Durability is a knob, not a cache: `Durability = Literal["sync", "async", "exit"]` — "'sync': Changes are persisted synchronously before the next step starts… 'exit': Changes are persisted only when the graph exits" (`types.py:89-95`). It trades write cost against how much gets re-executed after a crash. It never trades against LLM spend across runs.

**Node caching is content-keyed.** `CachePolicy.key_func` defaults to `default_cache_key`, documented as "Function to generate a cache key from the node's input. Defaults to hashing the input with pickle" (`types.py:521-529`), implemented as `pickle.dumps((_freeze(args), _freeze(kwargs)), protocol=5)` (`_internal/_cache.py:26-31`), with `_freeze` sorting mapping keys so `{"a":1,"b":2}` and `{"b":2,"a":1}` collide correctly. The composed key is `CacheKey(ns=(CACHE_NS_WRITES, identifier(proc), …), key=xxh3_128_hexdigest(args_key), ttl=…)` (`_algo.py:861-872`, `1170-1182`) — i.e. namespaced by node identity, keyed by a hash of that node's input value. Hits are served by `match_cached_writes()` splicing stored writes into the task and emitting them with `cached=True` (`pregel/_loop.py:1549-1566`). Docs frame it as cost/latency: `key_func` "defaults to a `hash` of the input with pickle", `ttl` "the time to live for the cache in seconds" ([graph-api](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api.md)).

**Dependency tracking:** none, explicitly. But content-keying buys *implicit* transitive invalidation along the value path — a node's input is the state the upstream nodes wrote, so an upstream change changes the hash and the cache misses. That only holds for dependencies that flow through state. Hidden inputs (clock, env, a database the node reads) are invisible to the key, which is why the cache carries a TTL rather than an invalidation protocol. It is value-propagation, not a dependency graph.

## Temporal — positional by construction, and the docs say so

Event History is "a complete, ordered log of everything that has already happened in a Workflow," and on replay "that result is reused, not recomputed. So Activities aren't executed again during replay" ([workflows](https://docs.temporal.io/workflows)). The matching rule is ordinal: "When the Workflow's code replays, the Commands that are emitted are compared with the existing Event History. If a corresponding Event already exists within the Event History that matches that command, then the Execution progresses" — otherwise "the Workflow Execution returns a *non-deterministic* error" ([workflow-definition](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-definition)). APIs that produce Commands "must not be reordered, added, or removed without proper Versioning techniques." That is the definition of position-keyed memoization: change the *order* of two activities whose inputs are identical and you break replay; change the *inputs* of an activity while keeping order and replay happily hands back the stale recorded result. Content is not consulted at all.

Scope is one Workflow Execution's history — there is no cross-run reuse of activity results. The nearest thing is dedupe at the workflow level: Workflow Id Reuse Policy (`AllowDuplicate` default, `RejectDuplicate`, …) and Conflict Policy `UseExisting`, which "Prevents the Workflow Execution from spawning and returns a successful response with the Open Workflow Execution's Run Id" ([workflowid-runid](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-execution/workflowid-runid)). That is idempotency on a caller-supplied id, not content addressing.

## DBOS — step-counter keyed, Postgres-backed

"Every workflow input and step output is durably stored in the system database," costing "one database write per step." On recovery DBOS "calls it with its checkpointed inputs. As the workflow re-executes, it checks before each step if that step's output is checkpointed in Postgres"; if so, "the step returns the checkpointed output instead of executing" ([architecture](https://docs.dbos.dev/architecture)). The contract that makes that safe is ordinal: "The workflow function must be deterministic: if executed multiple times, with the same arguments and step return values, the workflow should invoke the same steps with the same inputs in the same order," and "Steps should be idempotent." Cross-run dedupe again lives at the workflow id: "if a workflow is called multiple times with the same ID, it executes only once" ([workflow-tutorial](https://docs.dbos.dev/python/tutorials/workflow-tutorial)) — an explicit idempotency key, not a hash of arguments. Versioning is used to prevent replaying a journal into changed code: "DBOS versions applications and workflows so workflows only recover to processes running compatible code."

## Restate — journal index, per invocation

"The Restate SDK under-the-hood sends a message to the Restate server for each Context operation. The Restate Server then records it in the execution journal," and on replay "the SDK checks the journal for the last recorded result. If it finds a previous result, it skips executing that action and uses the recorded result instead" ([request-lifecycle](https://docs.restate.dev/guides/request-lifecycle.md)). Order of context operations is the key. `ctx.run` is documented as "the result is persisted in the journal and replayed on retries" ([durable-steps](https://docs.restate.dev/develop/ts/durable-steps.md)) — per invocation, not a shared cache; `ctx.rand.uuidv4()` / `ctx.date.now()` are seeded by invocation ID so non-determinism is journaled rather than re-rolled.

## Inngest — hash of the step id, plus its index

The most explicit statement of positional keying anywhere in this set: "The steps that successfully executed are *memoized*. The function then resumes, skipping any steps that have already been completed and the SDK injects the data returned by the previous step into the function," and "Internally, the SDK uses the hash of the step name to look up the result in the state data," with "the steps' index… also included in the result" ([how-functions-are-executed](https://www.inngest.com/docs/learn/how-functions-are-executed)). The reference page states the purpose of the id outright: it is "used to memoize step state across function versions" ([step-run](https://www.inngest.com/docs/reference/functions/step-run)). Rename a step and its memo is gone even though the work is byte-identical; keep the name and change what it does and the stale value is served.

## Cloudflare Workflows — same shape, stated as a rule

"Steps should be named deterministically (that is, not using the current date/time, randomness, etc.)"; "Because a step might be retried multiple times, your steps should (ideally) be idempotent"; a step that completed "after running successfully will not run again" ([rules-of-workflows](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workflows/build/rules-of-workflows/)). Step name is the cache key, explicitly.

## The contrast class: content-addressed memoization built to skip work

**Nextflow.** The task hash is "computed from the following metadata: Session ID, Task name, Task container image… Task inputs… Task script… Global variables referenced in the task script," and with `-resume` Nextflow "checks whether the task cache contains a matching hash and whether the task outputs are still present in the work directory. If both conditions are met, the task is resumed. Otherwise, it is re-executed." Invalidation is real and content-driven: "Nextflow calculates a hash for an input file using its full path, last modified timestamp, and file size. If any of these attributes change, Nextflow re-executes the task" ([cache-and-resume](https://docs.seqera.io/nextflow/cache-and-resume)). Because upstream outputs are downstream inputs, invalidation is transitive by construction — the canonical property none of the durable engines have. Note the Session ID in the hash: reuse is scoped to a resumed lineage, not global across users.

**Flyte.** Keyed on input literals — "task input values are taken into account to derive a cache key. This is done by turning the literal representation into a string and using that string as part of the cache key" — with a manual invalidation lever, "Bumping the `cache_version` is akin to invalidating the cache," and caching off by default "to avoid unintended consequences of caching tasks with side effects" ([flytesnacks task_cache.py](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flyteorg/flytesnacks/master/examples/development_lifecycle/development_lifecycle/task_cache.py)). Same family: content key plus an explicit code-version component, because the key can't see the function body.

**Model/tool caches in agent stacks.** LangChain's `BaseCache` is keyed on `(prompt, llm_string)` and the module docstring states the purpose flatly: "A cache is useful for two reasons: 1) It can save you money by reducing API calls if you're often requesting the same completion multiple times. 2) It can speed up your application" ([langchain_core/caches.py](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/langchain-ai/langchain/master/libs/core/langchain_core/caches.py)). LiteLLM: "LiteLLM's caching system stores and reuses LLM responses to save costs and reduce latency," with TTLs, a `x-litellm-cache-key` response header, `/cache/delete` for manual invalidation, and a pointed warning that semantic caching "is designed for single-shot prompts. On multi-turn or agentic traffic it will replay stale responses" ([proxy/caching](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/caching)). DSPy: "the cache key is derived from a hash of all request arguments sent to `litellm`, excluding credentials like `api_key`," LRU in memory plus `diskcache` on disk ([dspy.ai/tutorials/cache](https://dspy.ai/tutorials/cache/)). CrewAI caches tool results content-wise but only in process — `CacheHandler.add/read` key on `f"{tool}-{input}"` in a plain dict guarded by a lock, and declared failures are deliberately not stored (`lib/crewai/src/crewai/agents/cache/cache_handler.py`, main @ 9b1f493, 2026-08-17); nothing persists it across runs. And the provider-side mechanism — Anthropic prompt caching — is neither: it's a **prefix** match over the rendered `tools → system → messages` byte stream, where any byte change invalidates everything after it, with 5m/1h TTLs, ~0.1× read and 1.25×/2× write pricing. Position-keyed, but sold entirely on cost.

## What people actually use each for

Doc positioning is one-directional. Temporal's AI page sells "Guarantee all executions of all processes run to completion successfully in spite of failures" and "automatic retries out-of-the-box, and maintain the ability to retry until a probabilistic LLM returns valid data" ([temporal.io/solutions/ai](https://temporal.io/solutions/ai)) — it does not claim you stop re-paying for LLM calls. Restate's AI-agents page comes closest of the durable engines: "Persist steps (LLM calls, tools) and recover previous progress after failures," plus two cost lines that are about *not running* rather than *not recomputing* — "Suspend long-running agents when idle to save costs" and "Cap how many agent invocations run at once with flow control, putting a ceiling on LLM and API spend" ([restate use-cases/ai-agents](https://docs.restate.dev/use-cases/ai-agents)). The cache-layer docs invert this: LangChain leads with "save you money," LiteLLM with "save costs and reduce latency."

The billing models corroborate the split. Inngest charges per memoized unit — "An execution is a single durable function run plus each step inside it. If your function has 5 step.run() calls, one run uses 6 executions" ([pricing](https://www.inngest.com/pricing)) — and Temporal Cloud bills Actions, "the primary unit of consumption-based pricing… such as starting Workflows, recording a Heartbeat or sending messages" ([cloud/pricing](https://docs.temporal.io/cloud/pricing)). Adding a step to a durable engine costs money; adding an entry to a content cache saves it. These are opposite economic gradients, which is a structural reason durable engines are unlikely to grow into cost-saving memoizers.

## Bottom line

- **Established — keying.** Durable execution keys on position, universally, and the docs say so in their own words: Temporal matches Commands to History events in order and errors if you reorder or insert; Inngest hashes the step *name* and includes the step *index*; Cloudflare requires deterministic step *names*; DBOS requires "the same steps with the same inputs in the same order"; Restate looks up "the last recorded result" per context operation; LangGraph's task id is a hash of `(checkpoint_id, ns, step, node name, triggers)` with no input content in it. Content-keyed memoization exists in a different product category: Nextflow (inputs + script + container), Flyte (input literals + `cache_version`), LangChain/LiteLLM/DSPy (hash of the request), LangGraph's optional `CachePolicy` (pickle-hash of node input).
- **Established — transitive dependency tracking.** No durable-execution engine tracks it. Content-keyed pipeline tools get it structurally, because upstream outputs are downstream inputs and file hashes cover path/mtime/size (Nextflow states the re-execution rule explicitly). The agent-side caches get a weaker version: an upstream change invalidates only if it flows into the hashed input, which is why every one of them ships a TTL and a manual delete instead of an invalidation protocol.
- **Established — invalidation on upstream change.** Durable engines invalidate on *code shape*, not on data: Temporal Worker Versioning/patching, DBOS workflow versions, Inngest function versions. Changing an activity's inputs while leaving call order intact does not invalidate a recorded result — replay will serve the stale one. That is a correctness property nobody markets, and it is the sharpest single distinction from a memoizer.
- **Established — purpose.** Replay is sold and billed as reliability. LangGraph states outright that post-checkpoint nodes "re-execute, including any LLM calls." Inngest and Temporal charge per step/Action, so memoized units are a cost line, not a saving. The only cost language in durable-engine agent docs is about *suspending idle work* and *capping concurrency* (Restate), not about avoiding recomputation.
- **Contested.** Whether LangGraph's node cache is used in practice for dollars or only for dev-loop latency: the mechanism is content-keyed and the docs' example is a `time.sleep(2)` node, not an LLM call, and CrewAI's equivalent is in-process only. Also contested: whether provider-side prefix caching (position-keyed, cost-motivated) makes application-level content caching redundant for the dominant agent shape — LiteLLM's own warning that semantic caching "will replay stale responses" on agentic traffic argues the app layer is a poor fit there.
- **Unknown.** No public numbers on hit rates or dollars saved for any of these mechanisms — none of the vendors publish them and I ran no measurements. Unknown how often the stale-result-on-changed-inputs replay hazard actually bites in production (no incident data, and it would look like a wrong answer rather than an error). Unknown adoption share of LangGraph `CachePolicy` versus checkpointing. Unknown whether Flyte's current v2 docs changed the cache-key composition — the page 404s/renders empty at the union.ai URLs and only the flytesnacks example text was retrievable. Web-search budget was exhausted this session, so this is doc- and source-derived only; no community/forum signal on what users say they use it for.
