# What real build systems actually achieve

**Method note:** this session's web-search budget was exhausted, and every text-mode search engine (DuckDuckGo, Bing-via-fetch, Mojeek, searx, Startpage) either CAPTCHA'd or returned junk. I worked around it with a scripted browser, direct fetches of primary sources, and the GitHub API. Two of the four PDF/page summaries I pulled contained **fabricated quotes** (a "Taming Google-Scale Continuous Testing" fetch invented statistics like "over 500,000 test targets" for what is actually a John Micco slide deck), so I extracted and grepped the raw text of every load-bearing source myself. Every number below is quoted from text I read directly.

Because published population-level numbers turned out to be thin, I also **measured the effect myself** on two real repositories. Those measurements are the strongest part of this report and they independently reproduce the same shape.

## Published measurements

**Microsoft CloudBuild** (Esfahani et al., ESEC/FSE 2016) is the only peer-reviewed source I found that reports a cache hit rate over a real production build population — roughly 20,000 builds/day, of which ~25% are CI builds triggered by a code check-in. Verbatim: *"For 90% of the builds, at least 50% of the targets are cached, and for 50% of the builds, at least 80% of the targets are cached. The overall cache hit rate is 76%."* Separately: *"we have observed that 70 to 90% of build artifacts can be shared."* So the **median build reuses ~80% of targets and the population average is 76%** — not 98%. Caveat: it is a mixed workload including clean and user builds, and it is 10 years old.

**Gradle**, measuring its own CI (blog dated April 10, 2017, verified in-page): *"On average, we see a 25% reduction in total time spent building each commit, but some commits are even better (80% reduction) and the median build saw a 15% reduction."* This is a vendor measuring itself on its own project — maximally favorable conditions — and the self-reported **median is a 15% time reduction**. Note the unit: time saved, not fraction of targets reused. It is also nine years stale; I could not find a refreshed population figure from Develocity, whose current docs teach you how to read your own hit rate but publish no benchmark or target value.

**Uber's Go monorepo** (engineering blog, 2022, read in-browser) is the most useful qualitative datapoint. Their "Changed Targets Calculation" computes *"both 'directly' and 'indirectly' changed targets, which will all need to be retested and rebuilt"* — explicit transitive closure. The key verified sentences: a change that *"itself is only a few lines of code"* can mean *"validating this change could sometimes take several hours,"* and *"if a change has more than a certain number (say 10,000) of affected targets, then it is labeled a big change."* Against *"a repo with over 10,000,000 targets, most changes are small changes."* That is the whole story in one blog post: most changes are tiny, and the ones that aren't are catastrophic.

**Buck2** publishes no incrementality or cache-hit data at all. Meta's open-source announcement offers only *"Buck2 completed builds 2x as fast as Buck1"* — a vendor claim with no stated methodology, benchmark, or cache statistics. **Bazel** likewise publishes no population hit rates; its docs only explain how to read `remote cache hit` counts and attribute misses to *"something non-hermetic in the build causing the actions to receive different action keys."* **ccache** documents miss *causes* (`__DATE__`/`__TIME__` disabling direct mode, generated headers "too new", build-system-injected flags like a per-build UUID, compiler mtime changes) but no field hit rates; its own performance page only quantifies miss overhead at *"typically 5%-20%, but just 1%-3% with depend mode enabled."* One widely-cited practitioner post shows a 55.11% hit rate, but I checked the page and that figure comes from a **deliberately sabotaged demo repo**, not a field measurement — it should not be quoted as a real-world rate.

A warning on sourcing: searches for this topic surface a large volume of AI-generated content-farm pages (iancloud.ai, pistack.xyz, storypointlab.com, johal.in and similar) confidently asserting things like "cache hit rate on a well-bazelified codebase is typically 70–90%" or "60-90 percent faster." These have no methodology and no provenance. They are not evidence, and they appear to be the actual origin of most "typical build cache hit rate" folklore.

## My own measurements

**nixpkgs** — I pulled the CI-assigned rebuild-count labels for 1,000 merged PRs (2026-06-17 → 2026-08-17) via the GitHub API. The labels nest (a PR carries both `1` and `1-10`), so I computed the disjoint distribution per PR rather than trusting bucket totals:

| rebuilds caused | share of merged PRs |
|---|---|
| 0 | 7.3% |
| 1 | 47.7% |
| 2–10 | 30.3% |
| 11–100 | 7.4% |
| 101–500 | 1.1% |
| 501–5,000 | 1.2% |
| **5,001+** | **5.0%** |

85.3% of merged PRs rebuild ≤10 packages out of a repository of >100,000. But 5% rebuild more than 5,001. Weighting by work: **the top 5% of PRs account for 86% of all rebuild work** if you charge the tail its floor value of 5,001, and **~98%** if you charge stdenv-class changes their realistic ~50,000. Nixpkgs policy encodes exactly this asymmetry (verified verbatim in CONTRIBUTING.md): *"if the number of rebuilds is 500 or more, consider targeting the `staging` branch instead of `master`; if the number is 1000 or more, the pull request causes a mass rebuild."*

**PostgreSQL** — I built the transitive `#include` graph over 2,359 C/H files (15,408 includes, 4.7% unresolved), then replayed the last 300 real commits, computing for each the set of the 1,373 translation units invalidated:

- **Median commit: 1 file changed → 1 TU invalidated → 99.93% reuse.** The naive analogy holds exactly at the median.
- **Mean: 3.52% invalidated (96.5% reuse)** — 50x the median.
- p90 3.6%, **p95 27.1%**, **p99 55.3%**, max 100%.
- **The top 5% of commits carry 76% of all recompilation work; the top 10% carry 93%.**

Header fan-in is the mechanism: the median header is included by 7 TUs (0.5%), but p95 is 502 (36.6%) and `postgres_ext.h` reaches 1,238 (90.2%). Three concrete commits make it vivid:

- `da94518` "Drop support for `_MSC_VER` less than 1933" — **1 file changed** (`src/include/c.h`) → **1,232 TUs, 89.7% of the tree**. 1,232x amplification.
- `7a0299a` "Add a comment to distinguish backend types" — I read the diff: it adds **four lines of pure comment** to `miscadmin.h` → **492 TUs, 35.8%**.
- `catversion.h` was touched in 7 of 300 commits, each invalidating 757 TUs (55.1%). A version-stamp header with enormous fan-in, bumped routinely, whose content genuinely changes every time.

I also tested how much **early cutoff** (content-hashing rather than timestamping) rescues, by classifying header diffs that are comment/whitespace-only: it recovers only **9.1%** of total invalidation. So the amplification is overwhelmingly *real* dependency propagation, not dumb invalidation that a smarter cache would eliminate. Bazel and ccache would pay most of this too.

**Limits of my numbers:** the PostgreSQL graph resolves quoted includes only and drops 4.7%; it models compile-unit invalidation, not Bazel-style target or test granularity, so it is a good proxy for "fraction of work redone" but not a literal Bazel target count. The nixpkgs 5,001+ bucket is open-ended, which is why I bracketed it. Both windows are ~2 months.

## Bottom line

- **Established: the median small commit really does reuse ~99%+, so the analogy is directionally right about the typical case.** PostgreSQL's median commit invalidates 1 of 1,373 TUs; 85% of nixpkgs PRs rebuild ≤10 of >100,000 packages.
- **Established: the mean is nowhere near the median, and the mean is what you pay.** PostgreSQL mean invalidation is 50x its median; the top 5% of changes carry 76% (PostgreSQL) to 86–98% (nixpkgs) of all work. Two unrelated ecosystems, same shape. Any "98% saving" computed as an average over operations silently discards the tail that constitutes almost all of the cost.
- **Established: real measured population-level reuse lands well under the naive expectation.** CloudBuild's peer-reviewed 76% overall / 80% median-build, and Gradle's self-measured 15% median time reduction, are the only two real population figures I could find. Both are far from 98%.
- **Established: transitive fan-in is the dominant mechanism, not cache pathology.** Wide nodes — `c.h`, `catversion.h`, nixpkgs `stdenv` — mean a one-line edit legitimately invalidates 35–90% of the graph. Early cutoff recovers only ~9% of it in PostgreSQL. Non-determinism and timestamp effects (ccache's `__DATE__`, "header too new", injected UUIDs; CloudBuild's sandboxing to prevent "Frankenbuilds") are a real but second-order tax.
- **Contested: the widely-repeated "70–90% typical build cache hit rate."** CloudBuild's 70–90% refers to *shareable artifacts*, not hit rate, and its actual hit rate is 76%. The figure now circulates mainly via AI-generated content farms with no methodology. Treat it as folklore with one legitimate, decade-old ancestor.
- **Unknown: Bazel and Buck2 have no published incrementality or cache-hit statistics.** Meta offers "2x faster than Buck1" with no methodology; Google publishes none. Anyone citing a Bazel hit rate is citing a blog post about their own repo or an AI-written page.
- **Unknown: whether the shape transfers to the caching domain in question.** Build systems get something the analogy takes for granted — a *declared, machine-checked dependency graph* that computes the invalidation set exactly. Even with that luxury, the work distribution is so skewed that the average is ~50x the median. A domain that must *infer* what changed, without an explicit graph, has no reason to do better and every reason to do worse.

**The single most transferable finding:** in both ecosystems I measured, ~5% of changes account for 76–98% of the work. That means the headline "98% saving" and the actual expected saving are different numbers, and the gap is not a rounding error — it is the entire distribution. If the pitch computes savings as a per-operation average, it is measuring the median case and billing the tail to nobody.

# NEGATIVE SPACE

*What this experiment will not be able to establish, regardless of how cleanly it runs.*

The matrix (task families × δ ∈ {0, 2, 10, 30%} × 3 arms × warm/cold × seeds, real API, real usage counters, programmatic graders) is a good instrument for one question: *does dependency-tracked reuse produce a cost delta over provider caching in a controlled, hermetic, repetition-rich setting?* Almost every question a build/no-build decision actually rests on sits outside it. This section enumerates those, because a results table with tight error bars on the wrong estimand reads as more conclusive than it is.

---

## 1. Questions the harness structurally cannot answer

**1.1 The TTL-suppression rate, q — and it decides the sign.** Every reuse hit is a request the provider never sees, which stretches the inter-request gap and ages the provider's prefix toward expiry. The layer is net-negative once q > 1/(γ−1) — 19% at the field-measured γ = 6.27, 8.7% at γ = 12.5 (5m input line), 5.3% at γ = 20 (1h line). One induced cold miss cancels five to nineteen hits. A harness that *assigns* warm/cold as a factor has pinned, by construction, the single variable the conclusion turns on. Warm/cold is not an experimental condition in deployment; it is an *outcome* the reuse layer causes. Nothing in this design can observe that causal path, and the design will read as if it had.

**1.2 The real distribution of δ.** The harness produces a response curve at four experimenter-chosen points. Converting that to a dollar figure requires the traffic-weighted δ, which the harness cannot supply — and the world's δ is violently heavy-tailed. PostgreSQL: median commit invalidates 1 of 1,373 TUs (99.93% reuse), mean invalidation 3.52% (50× the median), p99 55.3%; the top 5% of commits carry 76% of all recompilation work. nixpkgs: 85.3% of merged PRs rebuild ≤10 of >100,000 packages, but 5.0% rebuild >5,001, and that 5% carries 86–98% of the work. A uniform grid over the body of the distribution measures the median case and misses the case that pays the bill. The mean is what you get invoiced for, and the mean is nowhere near any of the four grid points.

**1.3 Whether δ is even the right unit.** "2% of inputs changed" is not "2% of downstream work invalidated." Fan-in amplification is the entire mechanism: PostgreSQL commit `da94518` changed **one file** (`c.h`) and invalidated 1,232 TUs — 89.7% of the tree, 1,232× amplification; `7a0299a` added **four lines of comment** to `miscadmin.h` and invalidated 35.8%. Content-hashing/early-cutoff recovers only 9.1% of that, so it is real dependency propagation, not dumb invalidation. Unless the harness logs *realized* invalidation fraction alongside nominal δ, the x-axis is in a unit that does not map to the world monotonically.

**1.4 Anything about concurrency.** There is no fan-out axis. This omits the one measured, structural, non-TTL advantage in the entire evidence base: at 0 ms skew, five callers on one fresh prefix were **all five billed `cache_creation`, zero reads** (replicated), because "a cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins." Concurrent fan-out costs `w`× base — +25% (5m) / +100% (1h) — flat in N and flat in P, and never breaks even. In the field corpus 7.6% of tool repeats occur <1 s apart. A serial harness systematically *understates* the reuse arm, in a regime it never enters. It equally cannot tell you whether the win, when it appears, is really just single-flighting the prefix — a feature requiring no DAG, no store, and no dependency tracking, which 0/12 audited gateways ship.

**1.5 Staleness in deployment.** Staleness has exactly one cause: a real input to the operation that is not in the hash. A scripted harness is hermetic by construction — no env drift, no tool-version churn, no clock, no mutable external corpus. It will measure staleness ≈ 0 and that number will carry no information about production, where staleness lives entirely at leaves that read the outside world. The harness measures the one setting in which the key is complete.

**1.6 Correctness under a non-decidable equivalence predicate.** Programmatic graders make equivalence decidable. The literature's only clean zero-false-hit result (82% hit, 0 false hits on TPC-DS/SSB) was achieved precisely by making intent-equivalence decidable under strict schema validation; static-threshold semantic caches on free-form traffic run 1.7–4.1% error, *rising with corpus size*. The harness lives in the decidable regime and will report correctness as free.

**1.7 Any staleness bound on nondeterministic operations.** At temperature > 0, a shadow comparison measures staleness + resampling noise. Separating them needs a fresh-vs-fresh baseline arm at n ≈ 3,124 per arm to detect s = 1% against 2% intrinsic disagreement — ~31,000 at 20% disagreement, ~90,000 recomputations per window with the baseline arm's double execution. "Several seeds" is three to four orders of magnitude short. The experiment cannot claim a staleness bound on model calls at all; it can only claim a pass rate under its own grader.

**1.8 Statistical power on the only contrast that matters.** The decision-relevant quantity is arm3 − arm2, not arm3 − arm1. It will be small. With several seeds and unpaired sampling, the CI on that difference will be dominated by output-length lottery — output is 5× input price on every current Claude model, and output length is seed-sensitive while caching is not. Absent common random numbers across arms and a paired analysis, the harness will be measuring the sampler, not the cache. Separately: zero observed grader failures across k seeds bounds the error rate only at ~3/k (rule of three) — at k = 5 that is ≤ 45%.

**1.9 Arm decomposition.** The reuse arm bundles at least four mechanisms: (a) *not* marking prefixes that will never be reused (worth +24.8% avoided in the one-shot regime), (b) output-token reuse (no provider caches output), (c) non-model operation reuse (test runs, file reads, fetches — invisible to every provider), (d) prefix-equivalent reuse. If arm3 wins, the design cannot say which one won. That distinction is the product.

**1.10 Cost floors, volume regime, and integration cost.** The store's marginal cost is genuinely noise (~$2.17 per million ops on S3 Standard; break-even at one hit per ~13,400 ops), but the fixed floors are not — a $47/mo managed index against 10k cheap Haiku calls is 112% of model spend. The harness runs at one volume and cannot locate the floor. It also cannot measure the real cost of the product, which is the per-customer hunt for hidden inputs to make keys hermetic.

**1.11 Provider trajectory.** The result is a snapshot of an actively contested surface, measured on one rate card. Read discounts went 50% → 90% on OpenAI; extended 24h retention shipped free (Nov 2025), became the silent default (May 2026), then GPT-5.6 dropped it back to a 30m ceiling; Anthropic shipped automatic caching, cache diagnostics, and mid-conversation cache preservation — friction removal on exactly the surface a third-party layer sells into. The harness cannot estimate the half-life of its own conclusion.

**1.12 Multi-tenancy.** Caches are workspace-isolated (Claude API / AWS / Foundry) or org-isolated (Bedrock, Vertex, OpenAI). Pooling tenants creates cross-customer hits *and* a privacy problem; splitting them destroys the sharing you were counting on. Single-tenant harness, no axis, no answer.

**1.13 Latency and its price.** The harness measures money. Single-flighting costs a prefill; a reuse hit saves a full execution; a shadow check costs one. In agent workloads latency converts into human wait and additional turns. Not in scope, and it is half the value proposition of every comparable system (vLLM's own docs concede APC "does not reduce the time of generating new tokens").

## 2. Ways the result can be right about the measurement and wrong about the world

- **Manufactured repetition.** Scripted task families repeat prefixes far more than real agent traffic does. In 49,581 real billed requests, only **0.62% of model calls had an exactly-repeated full prefix** — agent conversations grow monotonically, so every turn is a novel prompt that merely *shares* a long prefix. Tool invocations do better (5.21% repeat). The reuse arm's hit rate in the harness is a property of the task generator. Exclusive addressable share after intersecting repeat rate with 1h-coldness: **0.137% of model calls, 1.58% of tool ops.**
- **A baseline nobody occupies.** Arm 1 (no cache) is a counterfactual with no buyer. Real shipped harnesses sit at 89–93% hit rates; the field corpus shows **96.45% of prompt tokens billed at the 0.1× read rate**, 85.3% saved versus no-cache. Any headline quoted against arm 1 describes savings the buyer already has. The published literature has the same defect — the one controlled academic study (Lumer et al., 640 sessions) *deliberately prepends a UUID to break the cache*, so its 78–80% reductions are total-value-of-caching, not incremental value.
- **Perturbation applied at the wrong nodes.** Randomly perturbing 2% of inputs samples the fan-in distribution uniformly; real edits concentrate on files people edit, and those include version-stamp headers with enormous fan-in (`catversion.h`: touched in 7 of 300 commits, 757 TUs each time). Uniform perturbation understates tail invalidation and therefore *overstates* reuse.
- **Warm/cold assigned instead of observed** (see 1.1). The world's cold-ness is partly caused by the treatment.
- **Grader-defined equivalence.** Users notice things graders don't score. A stale answer that passes the grader is a pass in the report and a support ticket in production.
- **Counters are not invoices.** Every dollar will be rate-card arithmetic over vendor-reported usage fields. No invoice has ever been reconciled against these counters in this repo. Enterprise discounts, committed-spend tiers, the Batch API's 50%, and priority tiers all move the multipliers — and the write premium (1.25× / 2×) versus read discount (0.1×) is precisely what determines whether marking a prefix is +25% or −32%.
- **Provider-dependent sign.** The write premium exists on Anthropic and GPT-5.6+, and *does not exist* on older OpenAI models, Gemini implicit caching, DeepSeek, or Fireworks. On free-write caches a concurrent fan-out forfeits a discount but incurs no premium — a materially different failure mode. A result measured on one provider does not port; DeepSeek already gives away hours-to-days automatic caching at a ~97% read discount, and vLLM/SGLang emit no token bill against which a saving can even be computed.
- **Seeds vary the sampler, not the world.** No variation in model version, provider-side routing, cache-node eviction pressure, workspace tenancy, or time of day (DeepSeek's peak/off-peak 2× is now live). The seed axis produces a precision estimate for a single point in a much larger space and will be read as a generalization estimate.

## 4. Gaps that flip a commercial decision even if the measurement is perfect

Ranked by how much of the decision they move.

1. **q.** Flips the *sign*, not the magnitude. Pinned by the design. If q > ~10% in real traffic, a perfectly-measured 20% harness win is a real-world loss, and the report will contain no evidence either way.
2. **Billability, not savings.** Contingent pricing (2–30% of savings) is available only where the provider's invoice settles the saving. A reuse hit is a call that *never happened*; it appears in no invoice. That likely caps the meter at the 0.2–1.0%-of-spend band the whole category converges on — a **10× revenue difference for identical delivered value**, decided by the meter and not by the measurement. A perfect savings number does not create a billable saving.
3. **Arm decomposition (1.9).** If the win is (a) — ROI-gated marking — the product is a policy, not a store: cheap to copy, already free in Anthropic's own SDK, and one of the five-of-twelve auto-injection features audited. If the win is (c) — non-model operation reuse — it is uncontested territory no provider touches, and the architecture is justified. Same number, opposite decisions.
4. **The δ tail.** The mean is 50× the median. A design tuned and priced on median-case reuse will be wrong by an order of magnitude on the invoices that matter.
5. **Provider move.** One Anthropic release-note line ("24-hour cache duration is now available") removes the last provider where a TTL-gap pitch lands. Nothing signals it — weak evidence, since OpenAI's 24h tier appeared with no advance signal at all. Equally: Anthropic shipping in-flight dedup would erase the fan-out advantage.
6. **Concurrency.** If the win reduces to single-flighting the prefix, the product is a day of work and the DAG is decoration.
7. **Baseline realism.** If headlines are quoted against arm 1, the buyer is sold savings they already realize, and churns on first invoice.
8. **Domain-stratified staleness.** A pooled aggregate bound licenses nothing. 0.5% staleness is free in CI triage (saturated with independent downstream checks; ~16% of Google's 4.2M tests are already flaky) and catastrophic in medical coding or claims. The pooled sample bounds only the aggregate; per-class bounds cost ~299 checks each, per window, forever.

## 5. Cheap changes that convert unanswerables into answerables

Pre-register these before the first run; each is hours, not weeks.

- Log **realized invalidation fraction** per trial, not just nominal δ; report cost against realized, and separately report the mapping δ → realized as a finding in its own right.
- Add **arm 2b**: provider cache with ROI-gated marking, no store. And **arm 3b**: store with model-call reuse disabled (non-model ops only). Without these the headline is unattributable.
- Use **common random numbers** across arms; analyze paired differences; power the design on arm3 − arm2, not arm3 − arm1.
- Add a minimal **concurrency factor** (N ∈ {1, 8} at 0 ms skew), even at two cells. It is the only place the mechanism has a documented structural edge.
- **Simulate q**: record the wall-clock gaps the reuse arm actually produces, replay them against the provider's TTL rules, and report the implied cold-write delta as an explicitly-flagged simulation. It is not a measurement of q, but it bounds it and it costs nothing.
- Record model id, rate-card date, workspace scoping, and minimum-cacheable-floor F per model. Publish cost as a formula in (w, r, F, TTL) with today's values substituted, so the result can be re-evaluated after the next provider change instead of re-run.
- State the **volume regime** and whether any fixed infrastructure floor is attached (content-addressed keys → $0 index; a managed index → a floor that can exceed model spend at small scale).

## 6. What a result of either sign will license

**A negative result is strong.** The harness is hermetic, repetition-rich, grader-decidable, and single-tenant — a maximally favorable setting. If arm3 does not beat arm2 here, it will not beat it in production, and that is a genuinely decisive, cheap finding.

**A positive result is weak, and its bias has unknown sign.** The design's distortions do not cancel, because they act on different axes: hermeticity and manufactured repetition inflate the reuse arm; the absence of concurrency and the pinning of q deflate it. The net is not a bounded bias around a true value — it is a point estimate whose direction of error cannot be signed from inside the experiment. The honest framing of a win is therefore: *"under controlled hermetic conditions with assigned cache state and no concurrency, reuse produced X% over provider caching; whether that survives contact with real arrival patterns depends on q, which this experiment cannot observe."*

Write that sentence into the abstract before the results exist, so it does not have to survive the temptation of a good number.
